The primary eclipses are occurring later over time while the secondary eclipses occur earlier than expected. This divergence in eclipse timing is a sign that the system is precessing.*

### 2.5 Refining the EB Sample for Precession Analysis

The initial cuts described in Section 2.1 reduce the full set of $\sim 2$ million TESS EBs to 12,819 systems suitable for further analysis. To identify those amenable to precession measurements, we apply several additional filters. First, because the typical EB period is $\sim 2.5$ days (Prša et al., 2011), many systems fall below the timescale where dynamical precession from a third body can be cleanly distinguished from tidal and rotational effects. We therefore exclude all binaries with orbital periods shorter than 3 days, removing 7,904 systems and leaving 4,915 longer-period EBs. Next, we require a minimum of two primary and two secondary eclipses to obtain a reliable precession rate and to avoid aliasing in the O $-$ C signal. Also, automated period and eclipse timing determinations fail in cases due to instrumental and astrophysical variabilities in the light curves. To identify these systems, we perform a visual inspection to confirm the cause. EBs are excluded when their light curves display large out-of-eclipse modulations (e.g. strong starspots, pulsations, flares, ellipsoidal variation, instrumental noise, contamination) that prevent a stable and repeatable mid-eclipse measurement. This step relies on by-eye vetting because the variability morphologies are diverse and not well captured by a single quantitative metic. A total of 3,325 EBs fail these requirements.

After applying these criteria, 1,590 EBs remain as our “clean" sample for initial O $-$ C inspection. From these systems, we identify 71 binaries that show clear signatures of apsidal precession, for which we perform the full precession rate calculation and dynamical inference presented in 2.6 and 2.7.

### 2.6 Calculating Precession

From the pool of precessing EBs, we quantify the precession, following Hilditch (2001) and Charbonneau et al. (2005), starting with the calculation of $e\cos{\omega}$ :

$$ e\cos{\omega}=\frac{\pi}{2P}(t_{\rm I}-t_{\rm II}-\frac{P}{2}+N\Delta P) $$

where $P$ is the average period of the eclipses, $t_{\rm I}$ is a mid-primary eclipse time, $t_{\rm II}$ is a mid-secondary eclipse time, and $N$ is the number of cycles between the eclipses. We calculate this value with two consecutive eclipses, so the last term goes to zero. Next, we calculate $e\sin{\omega}$ , again following Hilditch (2001) and Charbonneau et al. (2005):

$$ e\sin{\omega}\approx\frac{\Theta_{1}-\Theta_{2}}{\Theta_{1}+\Theta_{2}} $$

where $\Theta_{1}$ and $\Theta_{2}$ are the widths of the primary and secondary eclipses, respectively. The widths are measured by eye based on the total duration of the eclipse from the start of ingress to the end of egress. This expression implicitly assumes that eclipse durations depend primarily on orbital geometry through $\omega$ , but in practice they also depend on the impact parameter (or inclination) of each eclipse. Because we do not model the impact parameter explicitly, our estimates of $e\sin{\omega}$ carry additional systematic uncertainty. As a result, $e\cos{\omega}$ is significantly better constrained than $e\sin{\omega}$ , which we highlight as the dominant source of uncertainty in the derived eccentricities and arguments of periastron. With the results of equations 2 and 3, we calculate the eccentricity, $e$ . Using equation 2 at two different orbital cycles (typically the first and last observed), we measure $\frac{\text{d}}{dt}\left(e\cos{\omega}\right)$ , which can also be written as

$$ \frac{\text{d}}{dt}\left(e\cos{\omega}\right)=-e\dot{\omega}\sin{(\omega)}. $$

Rearranging gives

$$ \dot{\omega}=\frac{\text{d}}{dt}\left(\cos{\omega}\right)\frac{1}{\sin{\omega}}. $$

Here, we assume that the eccentricity $e$ remains approximately constant over the TESS observational baseline. This is generally a good approximation for hierarchical triples, where the apsidal precession timescale is much shorter than the eccentricity modulation timescale. However, perturbations from a third body can in principle induce measurable changes in $e$ over multi-year baselines (McKee & Montet, 2023, e.g.), so this assumption introduces an additional (usually small) systematic uncertainty.

The measured $\dot{\omega}$ therefore reflects the combined contributions from GR, tides and rotation, and any additional precession induced by a third body, all of which are additive. Here, we explicitly assume that all of these contributions act in the same (prograde) direction. This assumption is valid for the GR and tidal/rotational terms, and also for third-body perturbations, provided the system is not in a Kozai-Lidov (Kozai, 1962; Lidov, 1962) regime. In that case, the argument of periastron can exhibit more complex behaviour, like libration, rather than steady apsidal circulation. Thus, the precession due to a third body would be the difference between the total observed precession and that induced by tides and GR:

$$ \dot{\omega}_{\rm 3rd}=\dot{\omega}-\dot{\omega}_{\rm GR}-\dot{\omega}_{\rm CL} $$

where $\dot{\omega}_{\rm GR}$ and $\dot{\omega}_{\rm CL}$ are the precession due to GR and classical (tidal and rotational) effects, respectively. The precession due to GR, following Gimenez (1985) and Dimoff & Orosz (2023), can be written as:

$$ \dot{\omega}_{\rm GR}=(5.447127276\times 10^{-4})\left(\frac{1}{1-e_{2}}\right)\left(\frac{M_{1}+M_{2}}{P}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\text{ deg cycle}^{-1}. $$

$M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are the masses of the primary star and secondary star, respectively, in units of solar masses, and $P$ in units of days. As we only select systems which have been identified as main-sequence binaries, we use temperature values from Stassun et al. (2019) and temperature-mass relations from Eker et al. (2018) to determine the masses of the stars in the binary. Precession due to tidal and rotational effects, following Baroch et al. (2021), can be represented by:

$$ \dot{\omega}_{\rm CL}=360\times\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left(k_{i}c_{i}^{\rm rot}+k_{i}c_{i}^{\rm tid}\right)\text{ deg cycle}^{-1} $$

where $k_{i}$ is the internal structure (or apsidal) constant (Claret & Gimenez, 1993), which describes how mass is distributed inside a star; a star with centrally concentrated mass has a small $k$ (<0.02), whereas a star with a more uniform mass distribution has a larger $k$ (>0.1). We adopt $k_{i}=0.01$ as is used in the work of Kostov et al. (2021), adapted from the work of Torres et al. (2010) as an average value of the term for main sequence stars. This choice lies toward the high end of the range reported by Claret & Gimenez (1993), which spans $\log k_{i}\sim-3$ to $-1.9$ , corresponding to $k\lesssim 0.013$ . Adopting this upper-end value instead of our $k_{i}=0.01$ would increase $\dot{\omega}_{\rm CL}$ by at most a factor of $1.3$ . In most cases, the tidal and rotational contributions are the smallest component of the total precession budget, so this uncertainty does not significantly affect our calculations.

The rotational term, $c_{i}^{\rm rot}$ , following Baroch et al. (2021), is calculated as:

$$ c_{i}^{\rm rot}=\frac{r_{i}^{5}}{(1-e)^{2}}\left(1+\frac{M_{3-i}}{M_{i}}\right)\left(\frac{\Omega_{i}}{\Omega_{\rm m}}\right)^{2} $$

$\Omega_{i}$ and $\Omega_{\rm m}$ are the angular velocity of the star’s rotation and the angular velocity of its orbital motion, respectively. Tidal theory and observations both show that binaries with periods $\lesssim 10-12$ days are typically synchronised (Zahn, 1977; Meibom & Mathieu, 2005). We therefore assume $\Omega_{i}=\Omega_{\rm m}$ . $r_{i}$ is the ratio of the star’s radius to the semimajor axis of its orbit, where the radius is determined using temperature-radius relations from Eker et al. (2018) and the semimajor axis is determined through Kepler’s 3rd law and our precise determination of the binary’s orbital period. The tidal term, $c_{i}^{\rm tid}$ , following Baroch et al. (2021), can be expressed as:

$$ c_{i}^{\rm tid}=15r_{i}^{5}\frac{M_{3-i}\left(1+1.5e^{2}+0.125e^{4}\right)}{\left(1-e^{2}\right)^{5}} $$

A positive $\dot{\omega}_{\rm 3rd}$ value indicates that there is precession consistent with an additional perturbation caused by a third body in the system orbiting the EB. We classify the remaining systems with a positive $\dot{\omega}_{\rm 3rd}$ as candidate EBs to host a third body companion.

### 2.7 Defining Parameter Space of Third Body

The value of $\dot{\omega}_{\rm 3rd}$ allows us to determine the permitted parameter space for the mass and semimajor axis of the third body, following Miralda-Escudé (2002) using:

$$ \dot{\omega}_{\rm 3rd}=360\left(\frac{3M_{3}a_{\rm in}^{3}}{4(M_{1}+M_{2})a_{\rm out}^{3}}\right)\text{ deg cycle}^{-1} $$

where $a_{\rm out}$ is the perturber’s semimajor axis and $M_{3}$ is the mass of the perturber. We are especially interested in the region just outside the binary’s critical stability radius, given the high abundance of CBPs residing in this area.

The perturber could fall anywhere along the blue curve defined by Figure 4 outside of the critical radius. The lower mass limit, $M_{3,\textrm{min}}$ , is then determined as the point where the perturber parameter curve (blue line) intersects the critical radius (right edge of grey shaded region). The upper mass limit is poorly constrained at this point, but will be refined in future work (see Section 4.6 for more details).

## 3 Results

We visually inspect the O $-$ C and folded light curve plots of the 1,590 remaining systems and identify 71 as potentially exhibiting evidence of apsidal precession. This initial selection is based on the presence of a systematic and coherent divergence between the primary and secondary eclipse timing residuals over time, rather than random or noise-like scatter. In particular, we search for the characteristic anti-correlated pattern in which the O $-$ C curves of the primary and secondary eclipses evolve in opposite directions, as expected for apsidal motion. We do not require the signal to exceed a formal significance threshold at this stage, as our goal is to construct a candidate sample rather than a statistically complete census. This initial selection is solely to identify the targets that we analyse more carefully. After subtracting the terms $\dot{\omega}_{\rm GR}$ and $\dot{\omega}_{\rm CL}$ , 36 EBs remain with precession that cannot be accounted for by GR and tidal/rotational effects, outlined in Table 1.

Taken together, the 36 systems exhibiting residual apsidal precession and the 31 systems showing LTTE signatures imply that approximately 4% of the 1,590 inspected binaries display timing variations consistent with the presence of a third body. For comparison, in a survey of the Kepler EBs, (Rappaport et al., 2013) identified 39 triple-star candidates out of roughly 1000 EBs analysed, of which 15 host binaries have inner orbital periods longer than 3 days, matching the period range considered in our work. They further estimate that their detected sample represents roughly half of the true underlying population due to sensitivity and time-baseline limitations. Accounting for this incompleteness implies an effective occurrence rate of $3\%$ for triples among Kepler EBs with $P_{\rm Binary}>3$ days. Our inferred $\sim 4\%$ rate includes contributions from both stellar and possible planetary companions; restricting our sample to triple-star systems alone yields an occurrence rate of $\sim 2.5\%$ , in close agreement with the estimate of (Rappaport et al., 2013).

We also note 31 systems revealing evidence of the light travel time effect (LTTE); we provide the TIC ID’s and semi-amplitude values of the LTTE signal in Table 2. Otherwise known as the Rømer Delay (Rømer, 1677), LTTE is the observed shift in timing of both eclipses due to a change in the light’s path length to Earth as the barycentre of the binary wobbles around due to a third companion. Detectable LTTE in such cases would likely be caused by brown dwarf, stellar, or higher mass companions. Although these are interesting, the results of this paper focus on possible planet-mass companions. Thus, we focus on the 36 EBs in Table 1.

TIC 84546771 and TIC 198242678 both show signals that resemble fast, shorter-term precession likely caused by a more massive companion. TIC 115396972 is likely to have non-planetary-mass companions, as the minimum perturber mass lies right on the upper limit of a brown dwarf mass. We also exclude TIC 444544588 and TIC 167756615 due to their renormalised unit weight error (RUWE) from Gaia (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2021). A high RUWE value ( $>\sim 1.4$ ) suggests that the star’s motion is not well described by a single-star model, which is often a sign of an unresolved companion inducing detectable photocentre motion. For the systems in our sample, planet-mass companions at circumbinary separations near the stability limit are expected to induce astrometric signals far below Gaia’s detection threshold (typically tens of $\mu as$ ; Perryman 2011; Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016). Thus, Gaia RUWE is not sensitive to the types of CBPs we aim to detect. Likewise, the inner binaries themselves are unlikely to contribute significantly to the RUWE since the binaries we are looking at produce photocentre motions that are below Gaia’s resolution and are effectively averaged out over the mission baseline (Stassun & Torres, 2021). The RUWE for TIC 444544588 and TIC 167756615 are 2.45 and 2.23, respectively; therefore, they are likely to have a more massive companion. Although TIC 441496809, TIC 165615442, TIC 121092916, and TIC 342356517 exhibit apsidal precession consistent with a potential planetary-mass tertiary companion, their measured precession rates are all below a $3\sigma$ significance threshold. As such, we do not consider them candidates at this stage. Additional eclipse timing is required to confirm whether these systems host third bodies; for that reason, we exclude them from our candidate count. We therefore present 27 candidate circumbinary planets, with more than half permitting the existence of sub-Jupiter mass objects.

## 4 Discussion

In this work, we demonstrate that we can detect apsidal precession of EBs at a level of precision that enables the detection of sub-Jovian mass planets. We identify 27 systems that could host a planetary mass perturber, with over half allowing for sub-Jupiter mass. If the general population follows trends of the known CBPs, we can infer that the tertiary companions are likely to exist just outside of the critical radius of the binary. In this case, all 27 systems could be confirmed as CBPs. Refining the mass to rule out higher-mass companions is required for confirmation and relies on attaining RV data (see Section 4.6 for more information).

### 4.1 Comparison to the Known CBP Population

The 27 candidates identified in this work differ in several ways from the currently known CBPs discovered via transits. Transit surveys preferentially detect systems with cool, low-luminosity primaries, long eclipse durations, and deep transits; these biases make CBP discoveries strongly skewed towards Sun-like or cooler binaries. In contrast, our precession-based method is largely insensitive to stellar radius, luminosity, or transit depth. As a result, our sample includes a broader range of stellar types, including a fraction of hotter and larger systems for which transit detection would be extremely challenging. There are no known CBPs discovered by the transit method orbiting stars hotter than 6400 K, while 30% of our candidates are: the hottest stars in our sample have effective temperatures over 9000 K. Despite this, rapid rotation in these hotter stars is unlikely to produce spurious apsidal precession signals, as only 3 of the 36 precessing systems have both ${}_{T_{\rm eff}}>6300$ K and a tidal precession rate that is a non-negligible fraction ( $>10\%$ ) of the observed apsidal precession. Nevertheless, the role of tidal locking in these hotter stars is poorly constrained, and future measurements of stellar rotation ( $v\sin i$ ) will be important for directly assessing the influence of rotation on tidal effects in these systems. Additionally, the EBs in our sample have a wider range of orbital periods than the EBs with known CBPs: our shortest system has an orbital period of $4.2837\pm 0.0009$ days, while our longest has a period of $129.3214\pm 0.0008$ days, both outside of the range of periods of confirmed transiting planet-hosting CBPs. A full demographic comparison (distributions of perturber mass, inclination, etc.) is beyond the scope of this work but will be presented in future analyses.

### 4.2 LTTE and Precession

TIC 158330804, TIC 139699256, TIC 64366964, and TIC 146204045 show signs of LTTE in addition to the diverging precession signal in their O $-$ C diagrams (see Table 2 for semi-amplitude estimates). This double effect may be particularly informative, because the combination of apsidal precession and LTTE provides complementary constraints that can help break degeneracies in the inferred mass and orbital configuration of the tertiary companion. In principle, LTTE and apsidal precession could be produced by the same object or by two independent companions. Wider-baseline data or dynamical modelling is ultimately required to confirm or rule out multi-perturber configurations.

### 4.3 Short Term Variation

TIC 84546771 and TIC 198242678 both show short-term variations that require more follow-up to determine the cause of such precession. Possible causes of these signals include a very massive or nearby object. In both cases, the rapid evolution of the O $\textendash$ C curve suggests a dynamical influence that cannot be fully characterised with the current data. Continued timing monitoring and spectroscopic follow-up will be essential to determine whether these variations arise from a compact tertiary companion, dynamical interactions within a hierarchical system, or an alternative solution.

Short-term apsidal variation of this kind can be produced by (1) a massive tertiary on a moderately eccentric orbit, (2) resonant hierarchical architectures, or (3) combinations of multiple low-mass perturbers whose interactions are nonlinear over the TESS baseline. These systems are therefore strong candidates for full N-body dynamical modelling, but such work requires more precise constraints on the binary parameters. Future RV measurements and extended eclipse timing baselines are essential to determine whether these are unusual CBP configurations or more complex hierarchical triples.

### 4.4 Low-Mass Cases

The methods developed here allow for the detection of tertiary companions down to sub-Neptune masses. For several systems, specifically TIC 457579488, TIC 292357653, TIC 355503224, and TIC 158330804, the intersection of the perturbers allowed parameter space with the system’s critical radius permits solutions involving companions less massive than Neptune. A circumbinary planet of this mass would be the least massive detected to date, placing these systems at the frontier of current sensitivity limits. Continued monitoring and complementary follow-up observations are crucial for confirming such low-mass candidates and refining their orbital properties.

A natural question is whether these low-mass candidates are detectable through radial velocities alone. For a sub-Neptune mass CBP orbiting just outside the critical radius (typically 0.3-0.6 AU), the reflex velocity amplitude of the binary barycentre is not more than a few m s-1, even if the system is edge on. This magnitude places these planets near the limit of current state-of-the-art precision for surveys of bright systems such as BEBOP (Martin et al., 2019; Standing et al., 2022; Triaud et al., 2022). Thus, RVs may be able to place meaningful upper limits, but unambiguous planet detection may require a combination of long-baseline ETV monitoring, dynamical modelling, and astrometric constraints from future Gaia releases. In particular, while current Gaia data primarily provide summary diagnostics of non-single-star behaviour (e.g. RUWE), future data products will enable direct orbital modelling of tertiary companions, substantially improving sensitivity to low-mass and wide companions.

### 4.5 Mass–Separation Limits and Companion Types

Apsidal precession places limits on the mass–semimajor axis relationship of permitted companions, with the required mass to induce the observed precession growing as $a^{3}$ . Stellar tertiaries beyond a few AU would, if sufficiently massive, outshine the binary and be easily identified spectroscopically. Gaia astrometry already constrains the presence of stellar or brown-dwarf companions for many systems, and Gaia DR4 will significantly tighten these limits.

While our analysis assumes main-sequence tertiary companions, compact objects (white dwarfs, neutron stars, black holes) could in principle produce similar dynamical signatures. Most such companions at the relevant separations would produce detectable RV accelerations or Gaia astrometric motion. With the availability of epoch astrometry and RVs in Gaia DR4, it will become possible to directly test these scenarios on a system-by-system basis. Future observations will help determine whether any observed precession is caused by such compact objects.

### 4.6 Future Work

The 27 CBP candidates require follow-up radial velocity observations to refine their mass estimates and to rule out brown dwarf or stellar-mass tertiaries. All candidates are bright enough (T $<$ 13.5) for precise RV follow-up with modern 4–10 m class spectrographs. These systems therefore represent promising targets for future observing campaigns rather than relying on specific facility commitments.

Considering the sample we analysed was only a small fraction of the 2 million EBs in Gaia’s catalogue (Mowlavi et al., 2023), we anticipate many more detections as we expand this search across the larger sample. Additionally, combining the 7 year TESS data with past and future missions will increase the baseline of the search, and thus the sensitivity to small companions. Longer baselines will not only improve constraints on apsidal precession but also allow for the identification of multi-perturber systems and time-variable dynamical regimes that are currently indistinguishable within the existing data. Also, an in-depth transit search may find companions in these systems, making follow-up more straightforward. The combination of RVs, eclipse timing, Gaia epoch astrometry with DR4, and systematic transit searches has the potential to transform the circumbinary companion population from a handful of transiting planets to a statistically meaningful, dynamically rich sample.

## 5 Conclusions

Upon initial inspection of 1,590 eclipsing binaries from Gaia’s catalogue of over 2 million systems, we present 71 EBs that show signs of precession, 36 of which cannot be accounted for by effects due to general relativity and the rotational/tidal effects of the stars themselves. The calculation of precession was based on the change in the argument of periastron over time of the binary star, which can be determined by the exact timing of both primary and secondary eclipses. 27 of the 36 EBs may host a planet-mass companion in an outer orbit. We therefore present the discovery of 27 circumbinary planet candidates that induce apsidal precession on their host binary. Once further analysis is conducted to determine the perturber mass, we can confirm them as CBPs.

This method allows for the possibility of multiplying the number of known circumbinary planets because it is not limited in the orientation of the planet. It has the capability of detecting CBPs with higher mutual inclinations, therefore extending the sample to diverse architectures and orbital geometries. The findings of this work will allow us to robustly test formation theories, constrain migration histories, and understand long-term evolution of circumbinary systems.

# V347 Aurigae: from Peak to Quiescence

**Authors:** Diya T. Kumar Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, MC 249-17, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125; USA Email: diya@caltech.edu Lynne A. Hillenbrand Affiliation: Department of Astronomy, MC 249-17, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125; USA Email: lah@astro.caltech.edu Corresponding author: Lynne A. Hillenbrand Howard Isaacson Affiliation: Astronomy Department, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA Email: hisaacson@berkeley.edu

## Abstract

We present an analysis of eight epochs of high-resolution optical spectra of the YSO (young stellar object) V347 Aur. The source exhibits periodic brightness variations spanning $\sim$ 2 mag over several months, interpreted as cyclic accretion-burst and quiescent phases, making V347 Aur a useful probe of the broad range of accretion and outflow variability in YSOs. When faint, V347 Aur shows an M-type photospheric absorption spectrum; when bright, it exhibits a strong emission-line spectrum. Our Keck/HIRES spectroscopy was obtained during the decay of an accretion burst. The emission spectrum includes the strong H I, Ca II, and He I transitions commonly seen in YSOs, as well as numerous weaker metal lines, for which we provide a complete inventory. As the star fades, photospheric absorption lines deepen, consistent with decreasing veiling from the accretion continuum. H I and He I emission, which trace accretion, strengthen relative to the continuum as it fades, but show the expected decline in strength with decreasing accretion after correcting for the strong early veiling. Ca II behaves similarly, with line profiles that alternate between red- and blueshifted dominance, which we interpret as the rotation of the magnetospheric accretion flows. Narrow, slightly blueshifted absorption in Ca II, Na I, and K I indicates disk winds with localized density enhancements. Forbidden [O I] and [S II] emission is blueshifted, with broad shoulders and low- and high-velocity narrow peaks, consistent with a disk geometry that obscures much of the receding outflow. Their behavior as the continuum fades is similar to that of the broad accretion lines. The V347 Aur system is a useful proxy both for the ubiquitous short-term accretion variability observed in YSOs, and for their secular evolution on longer time scales.

#### Keywords:

## I Introduction

Young stellar objects (YSOs) are early-phase pre-main-sequence stars that often exhibit strong photometric and spectroscopic variability. This variability can arise from multiple physical processes including stellar rotation, surface magnetic activity, and most dramatically, unsteady accretion from a circumstellar disk onto the stellar surface [16]. The accretion flow is channeled from the inner disk to the star via the magnetosphere [26]. Empirically, there are correlated changes in accreting YSOs among photometric brightness, spectral lines that are diagnostic of disk-to-star accretion, and spectral lines that measure the strength and kinematics of outflowing winds and jets [14, 15, 4]. In some YSOs, accretion occurs in bursts or episodes, with variable accretion rates that are driven by instabilities in the magnetosphere or the inner disk [37, 12], or further out in the disk due to interactions with orbiting companions [36, 28]. These episodic accretion events can dramatically affect the observed source brightness, the spectral line profiles, and the continuum veiling.

V347 Aurigae is a highly variable, pre-main sequence star located in the small, isolated dark cloud L1438, about $200$ pc away. Flores et al. [17] determined stellar parameters of $T_{eff}=3200$ K, log g = 2.9 dex cm s-2, v sin $i$ =12 km s-1, and $B_{phot}$ = 1.3 kG. Donati et al. [11] derived similar values of $T_{eff}=3300$ K, log g = 3.3 dex cm s-2, v sin $i$ =12 km s-1, and also analyzed the source relative to stellar evolutionary models to find $M_{*}=0.33~M_{\odot}$ and $R_{*}=2.2~R_{\odot}$ with an inferred stellar age $<1$ Myr. Long-term archival photometry [10] revealed periodic brightness variations having large amplitude, about 2 magnitudes in the V band, that occur on a timescale of $\approx 160$ days, and that have persisted for decades. The star also illuminates a small reflection nebula that brightens and fades in coordination with the star’s photometric variability.

Spectroscopic observations [10] showed that during its photometric bright phases, V347 Aur displays an emission line spectrum that is dominated by strong HI Balmer, CaII, and HeI lines, weaker emission from FeI and FeII lines, and forbidden-lines of [OI] and [SII]. Absorption components are present in the wind-diagnostic lines of KI and NaD. In its fainter phases, the spectrum is dominated by absorption features from the underlying M-type photosphere. The presence of strong veiling during outburst phases, and the large variability in observed line strength and profile morphology, suggest large changes in the accretion rate between the faint and bright states. Giannini et al. [20] recently characterized low-resolution spectra of V347 Aur during both lower and higher accretion states. Their Figure 2 shows a strong emission-line spectrum in the blue optical even in a relatively quiescent accretion phase having $\dot{M}=10^{-7.71}~M_{\odot}$ /yr, compared to to $10^{-6.80}~M_{\odot}$ /yr during an active outburst. Donati et al. [11] sampled a broader range of accretion in V347 Aur, finding rates from $10^{-9.0}$ to $10^{-6.2}$ $~M_{\odot}$ /yr.

Dahm and Hillenbrand proposed that the recurring outbursts of V347 Aur could be in response to a companion or disk structure that periodically enhances the accretion rate. However, no companion was detected to the limits of the spectra under their study. [11] present the results of a 3.5 year monitoring campaign of V347 Aur using the SPIRou spectropolarimeter at CFHT and report that the source is in fact an eccentric binary system, refining the period value to $154\pm 0.7$ days. These authors provide evidence for a brown dwarf companion having a mass of $29\pm 1.6~M_{\rm Jup}$ and an eccentricity of $0.28\pm 0.12$ , confirming the earlier hypothesis by Dahm and Hillenbrand that a companion may be responsible for triggering the observed periodic accretion bursts. The intensity of emission lines was found to vary significantly, with episodes of strong veiling detected during bright phases. [11] also found that strong to extreme accretion events were occurring near the orbit periastron.

In this paper, we present an analysis of high-resolution optical spectra collected with Keck/HIRES for V347 Aur. The data were obtained over a time span of approximately 3 months relative to the $\sim$ 5 month full cycle. The spectra capture the system during its decline from a photometric maximum into quiescence. By tracking the time evolution of the spectral lines, we characterize how the veiling, accretion flow, and wind structure evolve throughout the outburst. The changes we see are presumed to measure a decrease in the disk-to-star accretion rate, the accompanying cooling of the accretion shock at the stellar surface, and a decrease in the accretion-driven wind.

Studying V347 Aurigae in this detail provides an opportunity to investigate a system that contains several unusual properties. First, V347 Aurigae is an M-type pre-main star that is completely isolated [10], representing a different environment than the clusters in which most stars form. Second, the presence of a close brown dwarf companion represents a relatively uncommon configuration [30, 2]. Third, its periodic and sustained outbursts make V347 Aurigae a valuable system to study since it can be monitored over complete cycles that sample high to low accretion states. The connection between the photometric evolution of the outbursts and the emission-line spectrum has not yet been explored, however. Our time-series spectroscopy covers the decline from photometric maximum and thus allow us to track the evolution of individual spectral features while distinguishing changes in veiling from the line-profile behavior. Mapping these spectral changes across the order-of-magnitude changes in the accretion rate can inform our understanding of the accretion-dependent properties of YSOs more generally. The V347 Aur system is a useful proxy both for the ubiquitous short-term accretion variability seen in YSOs, in which the changes exhibited by different objects range over several orders of magnitude in their amplitudes and in their time scales, and for the general case of accretion and outflow in YSOs, where mass flow rates among large samples span 1.5 dex at any given stellar mass and age.

In Section 2 we present the source light curve and describe our spectroscopic dataset. In Section 3 we present our methods in characterizing the spectral changes over time, followed in Section 4 by the results of our line-by-line analysis. Section 5 provides a discussion of the findings, and our summary appears in Section 6.

### II.2 High Dispersion Spectroscopy

The Keck/HIRES [40] spectroscopic data set is available through the Keck Observatory Archive and was obtained using the infrastructure of the California Planet Search11 1 https://california-planet-search.github.io/. This includes observations, image processing, spectral extraction to one-dimensional format, and wavelength calibration, all as described in [23]. HIRES provides broad optical coverage across three detectors. In the utilized setup, the blue $b$ chip spans $\sim$ 3600-4800Å, the red $r$ chip $\sim$ 5000-6430Å, and the “infrared” $i$ chip $\sim$ 6500-7990Å. The achieved spectral resolution R $\approx$ 60,000 ( $\Delta v\approx 5$ km/s).

The spectra were obtained on eight separate nights between November 19, 2021, and February 16, 2022, capturing the star at various stages during its decline from outburst (see Figure 1). The collection times span the post-outburst fading, including a brief re-brightening between the first and second epochs, a subsequent local maximum during the decline, the continued decline into quiescence, and finally in the quiescent state itself. This temporal coverage enables a detailed view of the evolving spectral line behavior across a factor of nearly 4 in brightness (from 12.42 mag to 13.88 mag).

Typical integration times were 300 seconds and resulted in signal-to-noise ratios ranging from $\sim$ 3-15 in $b$ , $\sim$ 4-33 in $r$ , and $\sim$ 31-71 in CCD $i$ . Table 1 summarizes the observational details, including the corresponding source magnitudes, the realized signal-to-noise ratios across the three CCD bands, and the barycentric velocity corrections for each epoch.

## III Methods

### III.1 Spectral Pre-Processing

The extracted spectra are stored in a FITS format, with wavelength and flux values read using the Astropy package. Each of our eight spectra have their own wavelength calibration, thus for a fixed order, individual spectra can exhibit small differences in wavelength coverage and sampling. We therefore interpolated each spectrum onto a common wavelength grid that covers the overlapping wavelength range, resulting in a uniform wavelength spacing (Å per pixel) across the order.

After interpolation to the common wavelength grid, the following set of processing steps were applied to clean and standardize the data: outlier removal, smoothing, continuum fitting, and velocity corrections.

To remove outliers, flux values deviating beyond ten standard deviations from the median in each order were masked. For visual clarity in plotting, a gaussian filter was applied to some of the lower signal-to-noise spectra at later epochs (see Table 1) using the scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter1d routine.

To normalize the spectra, individual spectra were divided by the observed flux in a fitted continuum around spectral lines of interest. For spectral regions where the continuum showed a noticeable slope, a first order polynomial was used. Orders with a relatively flat continuum were fit with a zeroth order polynomial. The choice of polynomial order was based on the visual inspection of the shape of the baseline.

To center spectral lines in the stellocentric reference frame, we applied velocity corrections to the individual spectra that take them from the rest frame of the telescope to the rest frame of the star. We have accounted for both the barycentric corrections tabulated in Table 1, and the radial velocity of the source relative to the Sun. For latter, we have applied a correction of -8.9 km/s, adopting the +8.9 km/s radial velocity found from cross correlation by [10], which is consistent with the +8.6 km/s median radial velocity reported by [11] based on LSD analysis.

We validated the corrections by examining isolated atomic absorption lines in our spectra. These are sparse in number, given the heavy veiling for the earlier epochs and the cool photosphere dominated by TiO that is seen in the last few epochs. In the reddest wavelengths of our spectra, we could identify several plausible lines (Ca I 7326.15 Å, Fe I 7401.69 Å, Cr I 7400.18 Å, and Rb I 7800.27 Å) for this purpose, detected only in the later epochs. The most useful for our purpose is the Rb I line, which is a member of a resonance doublet (the other line at 7947.60 Å is contaminated by TiO) and easily ionized, so it is typically seen only in very late M and L type dwarfs. Rb I is also gravity-dependent [31], perhaps explaining its visibility in V347 Aur at an earlier spectral type (M4) and young age. Although weak, with equivalent width only $\sim$ 0.1 A, Rb I 7800.27 reaches a depth of 25% below the continuum, and the line is perfectly centered in velocity space – confirming our heliocentric and radial velocity corrections.

### III.2 Spectral Analysis

To identify spectral lines, we use the find_peaks function from the scipy.signal module, which detects local maxima in the flux values. The peaks were identified using thresholds on prominence and minimum distance, to ensure that only significant spectral features that were well separated from neighboring maxima were classified as true emission lines. For this analysis, we use the spectrum collected on 2021-12-17. This particular spectrum does not have the highest signal-to-noise ratio, but it provides a particularly favorable view of the emission line inventory, as it corresponds to a local maximum in the light curve.

A tabulation of detected emission lines appears in Appendix A. In the analysis below we focus on a few of the most prominent emission lines. However, in its outburst phases, V347 Aur exhibits a rich spectrum of emission lines consisting mainly of weak Fe I and Fe II lines, but also Ti I and Ti II, Cr I, and Cr II, Ca I, and Mg I features.

Equivalent widths were computed using the specutils.equivalent_width function applied to continuum-normalized spectra. We performed a direct numerical integration of the line profile over defined wavelength regions.

To quantify the errors on the equivalent width measurements, we adapt a formula from [41]. However, we modify their formula to account for the fact that our lines are in emission rather than absorption, and also are generally much stronger in equivalent width than their typical wavelength interval $\Delta\lambda$ .

We also substituted half of the line peak flux for the average spectral line flux. The lines of interest in this work are typically strong, broad and non-gaussian in shape, with average flux that is thus significantly decreased relative to a gaussian line.

Our modified equation for the equivalent width error is:

$$ \sigma(W_{\lambda})=\left|\sqrt{1+\frac{\overline{F_{c}}}{\frac{1}{2}\times F_{max}}}\cdot\frac{\Delta\lambda-|W_{\lambda}|}{S/N}\right|. $$

In the interpretation of the declining light curve from outburst peak (Figure 1) as a decrease in accretion rate, we can expect that observed equivalent widths are affected by changes to the continuum veiling. Continuum veiling is denoted by the veiling parameter $r$ , defined as the ratio of the excess continuum flux to the intrinsic photospheric continuum flux [21]. The presence of excess continuum reduces the apparent equivalent widths of photospheric absorption lines such that $EW_{true}=EW_{observed}\times(1+r)$ . The veiling factor for each epoch was measured using the least veiled epoch as the reference photospheric spectrum. We account for changes in continuum veiling by applying this multiplicative correction to the measured equivalent widths. We also propagate the $1+r$ factor in the errors. At early epochs, the total error is dominated by the large veiling values, while at later epochs the lower signal-to-noise contributes most of the total error.

As mentioned above, photospheric absorption is prominent in only the last few epochs of our data set. The high level of veiling during the early epochs means that there are few regions of spectrum that are viable for the measurements. We fit two regions: the continuum-normalized Li I 6707 Å line profile, and the entire order containing the broad TiO 7100 and 7140 Å bands. The best fitting value of $r$ was chosen for each epoch by minimizing the $\chi^{2}$ difference between a model consisting of a veiled version of the final epoch, and the observed spectrum. The veiling values from the two regions are broadly similar, except at the earliest epochs when the veiling values are largest, with the Li I measurements about 50% higher. We adopted the TiO based values, which we consider more reliable given that they were derived over a wider range of the spectrum. Both sets of measurements are presented in Table 2.

In applying a veiling correction, we adopt the approximation that veiling is independent of wavelength across the spectral range of our dataset. This has been demonstrated for wavelengths $>5500$ Å observationally [6] and is true theoretically for veiling values up to around 5 [34]. While veiling may increase towards shorter wavelengths, the limited number of absorption lines exhibited by V347 Aur at the earlier epochs do not allow us to measure a wavelength-dependent veiling correction.

Finally, to analyze the spectral lines in velocity space, we apply the doppler formula. This transformation allows us to use the morphology of spectral lines to track the motions of gas in the system over time.

### III.3 Quantifying the Time Evolution of Spectral Lines

For each identified spectral line, we analyze its temporal evolution across epochs by measuring several key properties, including line center shifts, line broadening, observed line strength, and line structure.

Line center shifts are quantified by tracking changes over time in the wavelength of peak flux, which indicate gas motion. Line broadening is characterized using the full width at half maximum (FWHM), which can indicate the thermal motion of the gas and the rotation of the star. Line strength is measured through equivalent width calculations, corrected for veiling, that quantify variations in the density of absorbing or emitting atoms. Finally, changes in line structure are visually examined in the wavelength and velocity plots.

## IV Line Analysis Results

Our analysis of spectral evolution in V347 Aur is separated into three categories. We first study absorption features, focusing on TiO and Li I 6707Å which are the most prominent. We then study the strong emission lines, including lines of hydrogen, helium, calcium, and iron. Finally, we study several outflow diagnostics of slow winds and fast jets.

The specific emission lines for which we present line profile time series are: H $\alpha$ , H $\delta$ , H $\gamma$ , HeI 5875.62 Å, HeI 6678.15 Å, CaII 3968.47 Å, CaII 3933.66 Å, FeI 5455.61 Å, and FeII 5316.62 Å for the strong (predominantly accretion) lines; and KI 7698.96 Å, NaD 5895.94 Å, [OI] 6300.30 Å, and [SII] 6730.82 Å for the wind/jet diagnostics.

The earlier spectra towards the bottom of the figure (e.g., 2021-11-19, 2021-11-24) show a veiled continuum with minimal to no absorption and weak emission lines, consistent with strong accretion activity. In contrast, later spectra towards the top of the figure (e.g., 2022-01-08, 2022-02-16) exhibit deep photospheric absorption features, reflecting the decreasing veiling as accretion subsides.*

The legend includes the number of days since peak brightness. As the source fades, the veiling decreases, and the line absorption deepens.*

### IV.1 Photospheric Absorption Features

As V347 Aur fades into quiescence (Figure 1), absorption features in the spectrum become more pronounced. Figure 2 illustrates the TiO band region around 7100 Å. The later-in-time and fainter epochs show spectra with deeper absorption features. These may be compared to the earlier-in-time and brighter epochs when the spectra are more heavily veiled, and there is even weak emission in some atomic lines.

This observation signals a decline in the continuum veiling of spectral absorption lines that is caused by accretion activity. During periods of high accretion, excess continuum emission veils the absorption lines, making them appear shallower. As the accretion rate drops and veiling decreases, the photospheric absorption becomes more apparent. As noted above, atomic absorption lines are difficult to see in V347 Aur. Our analysis below includes only Li I, which is the most prominent absorption line aside from the broad features due to TiO.

Li I centered at 6707.856 Å is usually a prominent absorption line in YSO spectra. This line is expected from theory to be preserved in young stars, for at least some portion of their pre-main sequence lifetimes. In these fully convective stars, photospheric lithium is efficiently transported throughout the stellar interior, where it is destroyed. As a result, the strength of lithium serves as an indicator of stellar youth [24, 38, 44].

In V347 Aur, the Li I feature (Figure 3) apparently strengthens as the star fades. The exception to the observed trend is the 2021-12-17 epoch, in which the line is the weakest. This particular spectrum coincides with a small photometric re-brightening (Figure 1) and probably reflects a short-lived episode of heightened accretion activity. The Li I 6707.856 Å line is a doublet, which even becomes visibly resolved in V347 Aur in the final epoch (gray) as the veiling decreases and the profile sharpens. We note that in stars with large v sini, the nearby Fe I lines at 6704.48 and 6705.11 Å on the blue side and the weaker 6711.30 Å on the red side can blend in and contaminate the observed Li I profile. However, given V347 Aur’s v sini of $12.0\pm 0.5$ km s-1 [11], these Fe I lines are not a significant contaminant here. The velocity profile shows that Li I is consistently centered on the stellar rest velocity across all epochs.

To illustrate the effect of the veiling correction, Figure 3 displays both the measured and the veiling-corrected equivalent widths. The apparent increase in observed equivalent width towards later epochs is reduced or removed after applying the correction, yielding line strengths that are approximately constant within the uncertainties. This shows that the adopted veiling-correction procedure based on the TiO region recovers the expected instrinsic photospheric line strength, within the errors. We note that for the 2021-12-17 spectrum, the measured equivalent width of the Li I line is positive, despite the line core being in absorption; this arises because of the broad equivalent width integration range. As emission is unphysical for this line, and inconsistent with visual examination, we have set the corrected equivalent width at this epoch to zero.

### IV.2 Strong Emission Lines

#### IV.2.1 Hydrogen Balmer Lines

*Figure 4: Spectra around the H-alpha line at 6562.80 Å (top), H-gamma at 4340.50 Å (middle), and H-delta at 4101.70 Å (bottom). Left panels show observed, continuum-normalized spectra while middle panels are velocity plots where we omit the last spectrum in the H-gamma and H-delta plots due to noise in the continuum. The right panels show equivalent widths; open circles denote the measured values, while filled circles (connected by a dashed line) denote the veiling-corrected values. For visual clarity, the measured (open) equivalent width measurements at later epochs have been offset by 0.05 magnitudes to avoid overlapping error bars with their veiling-corrected (filled) counterparts. As the star fades over time, the spectral lines become broader with enhanced blue-side emission. In addition, some peaks change their morphology into multiple peaks, especially in H-alpha, or are seen to shift in the location of their peaks, for H-gamma and H-delta. The observed line profiles relative to the continuum level generally increase as the star fades, but the veiling-corrected equivalent widths illustrate that the line strengths are actually decreasing.*

The Hydrogen Balmer lines are usually strong emission features in spectra of YSOs. Our V347 Aur data set includes the H $\alpha$ , H $\gamma$ , and H $\delta$ members of the Balmer series; unfortunately, H $\beta$ falls outside the spectral coverage, between orders on the detector. The Balmer line profiles show signatures of both accreting and outflowing material, with their morphology evolving significantly as V347 Aurigae fades.

As shown in Figure 4, the Balmer lines broaden and shift to shorter wavelengths as the star fades. The evolution of the line profile shape seems to differ between lines. As seen most prominently in H $\alpha$ , a distinct asymmetry towards the red in the emission line profiles is present in the earlier observations, while towards the later observations, more blue-side emission becomes apparent. The 2021-11-28 spectrum, taken near a photometric local minimum shows mild blueshifting, and the final four epochs show more evidence of it. The last epoch (2022-02-16) is omitted for H $\gamma$ and H $\delta$ due to low signal-to-noise. As the star fades, these lines show growth in their blue-side emission relative to the red-side (Figure 4). The increasing blue-side emission is consistent with the increased visibility of outflowing material. As the accretion decreases, the emission from wind-related components moving towards the observer becomes more apparent.

The H $\alpha$ profile also has a complex, multi-component structure, with various narrow blueshifted absorption that are transiently seen against the broad emission profile. By the 2021-12-26 spectrum, the blueshifted side of the profile starts to broaden. In the final three epochs, the line exhibits multiple blueshifted peaks, growing to two separate peaks. In contrast, H $\delta$ and H $\gamma$ initially appear as double-peaked profiles with their blueshifted components at -50 km/s and their redshifted components at 100 km/s and 70 km/s respectively (measured from the first collected spectra). Additionally, for H $\gamma$ , the redshifted peak is about 1.3 times stronger than the blueshifted one at onset, but the blueshifted peak grows taller than the redshifted one, becoming about 1.5 times stronger. For H $\delta$ , the redshifted peak is initially taller than the blueshifted one, by a factor of about 1.16, and the blueshifted peak then grows to about 1.28 times stronger than the redshifted peak. In both of these lines, in the 2022-01-19 spectrum, the double peak disappears and only a single, stronger blueshifted peak is present. As noted above, the final epoch for H $\gamma$ and H $\delta$ (2022-02-16) is omitted in the plots due to low signal-to-noise.

These variations are further quantified through equivalent width measurements, displayed in Figure 4. In every line, the observed line-to-continuum strengths generally increase as the star gets fainter, but the veiling-corrected equivalent widths generally decrease, as expected. The absolute scale also drops sharply down the Balmer sequence, as expected. We note that rather than a smooth monotonic decline, all three lines show a partial rebound at the 2021-12-17 epoch, likely linked to the brief photometric re-brightening at that time.

#### IV.2.2 Calcium H&K Lines

*Figure 5: Spectra and equivalent width measurements of the CaII line centered at 3968.47 Å (top panels) and 3933.660 Å (bottom panels), similar to Figure 4. As the star fades, the CaII lines become stronger in terms of line-to-continuum, except in the last spectrum. The veiling-corrected equivalent widths show a general correlation between source brightness and line strength.*

In addition to the hydrogen Balmer lines, the Ca II H&K doublet lines are also typically strong lines in YSO spectra. V347 Aur is no exception, and its Ca II lines exhibit substantial variability over time, with profiles showing two prominent peaks whose relative strengths and velocity structure evolve as the system fades. We note that the 3968.47 Å Ca II H line likely has some contamination on its red side from hydrogen $H\epsilon$ at 3970.08 Å, which will have a morphology and strength that changes over time as discussed above for the other H I lines. The 3933.66 Å Ca II K profile is free of such contamination. Unfortunately the Ca II “infrared triplet” is outside the wavelength coverage of our particular HIRES setting.

Figure 5 shows that the 3968.47 Å and 3933.66 Å lines become progressively stronger in terms of line-to-continuum, and more sharply peaked as the star fades. This trend is interrupted twice: at the 2021-11-28 epoch, the line-to-continuum strength is anomalously high relative to its neighboring epochs, particularly in the 3933.66 Å line; and at the 2021-12-17 epoch, the profile briefly reverts to a wider, flatter morphology, coincident with a small photometric rebrightening. The line continues sharpening over the following three epochs before the final epoch where it returns to a broader and weaker morphology similar to that seen when the star was at its brightest.

The velocity structure of the peaks is also notable. For the 3968.47 Å line, the taller peak is blueshifted and the shorter peak is redshifted. However, for the 3933.66 Å line, the taller peak is redshifted and the shorter peak is blueshifted. As the star fades further, particularly around the 2022-01-19 epoch, this pattern reverses, with the taller peak becoming blueshifted, to match the velocity structure of the 3968.47 Å line. This behavior is similar to that of H $\delta$ and H $\gamma$ , where the velocity structure switches from being primarily redshifted to blueshifted.

We also call attention to two narrow absorption lines against the broad peaks of the Ca II lines, that increase in strength as the star fades. In the earliest spectrum, the more prominent of the two features is located at -6.6 km/s with a FWHM of 6.8 km/s in the 3968.47 Å line, and at -9.7 km/s with a FWHM of 8 km/s in the 3933.66 Å line. The absorption feature does not show significant signs of broadening, and the velocity of the line stays constant throughout its evolution. The second, higher velocity absorption component is at -28.8 km/s with a FWHM of 6.4 km/s for the 3968.47 Å line, and at -31.9 km/s with a FWHM of 4.7 km/s for the 3933.66 Å line. In contrast to the lower velocity absorption feature, this feature shifts slightly redward as the star fades. The narrow absorption components generally deepen as the star fades, with some exceptions.

Figure 5 shows the measured and veiling corrected equivalent widths of both Ca II lines (right panels). As with the Balmer series, these lines show an overall decline in veiling-corrected emission strength as the source fades, consistent with a decrease in accretion-related veiling even though the line-to-continuum has increased (center and right panels).

#### IV.2.3 Helium Lines

*Figure 6: Spectra and equivalent widths for the He I 5875.65 Å line (top) and the 6678.15 Å line (bottom), similar to Figure 4. In general, as the star fades the He I 5875.65 Å line becomes stronger relative to the continuum, and more sharply peaked. The HeI 6678.15 Å profile initially follows this behavior, but then likely becomes influenced by the FeI that contributes at this same wavelength. The veiling-corrected line strengths decrease over time as the source fades.*

Helium emission is not as ubiquitous as hydrogen and ionized calcium emission in young stars, but is typically present for strong accretors. As V347 Aur fades, the He I lines at 5875.65 Å and 6678.15 Å in our spectra exhibit subtle changes in shape and velocity. The line strengths change more significantly.

He I is typically decomposed into two parts: the broad component (BC), which describes the base of the line, and the narrow component (NC), which describes the peak near line center [7]. As shown in Figure 6, the shape and strength of the observed BC’s of the 5875.65 Å and 6678.15 Å lines do not change between epochs. However, the observed NC of both lines does change across epochs, driving the equivalent width changes presented in Figure 6.

The 5875.65 Å line roughly follows the same trends as the Balmer lines, with the lines becoming stronger in terms of line-to-continuum as the star fades (with some exceptions in the 2021-12-17, 2022-01-08, and 2022-02-16 spectra). The line-to-continuum strength of the 6678.15 Å line also increases as the star fades, with the exception of the final three spectra. We note that the 6678.15 Å He I line is coincident with an Fe I line, which may influence the behavior at later epochs. The veiling-corrected He I line strengths (right panels) generally decrease in strength as the star fades, similar to the H I Balmer and Ca II lines.

In terms of shape, for both lines, as time progresses, rather than strictly following the star’s brightness, the line peak shifts from being slightly redshifted to slightly blueshifted, transitioning in the 2021-12-17 spectrum. In the final spectrum, the peak of the 5875.65 Å line shifts back toward the center, appearing slightly redshifted again. For the 6678.15 Å line, the peak stays slightly blueshifted.

#### IV.2.4 Iron Lines

*Figure 7: Spectra and equivalent widths for the FeI line at 5455.61 Å (top) and the FeII line at 5316.62 Å (bottom), similar to Figure 4. Both lines decrease in terms of both line-to-continuum and veiling-corrected line strength as the star fades. We note the blueshifted asymmetry in the 2021-11-28 spectrum, which is not seen in the other line species.*

V347 Aur has a rich metal line emission spectrum (Appendix A), with many of the lines identifiable as Fe I or Fe II. We have chosen one of each as representative. The equivalent widths presented in Figure 7 illustrate the declining strength of both Fe I and Fe II emission, with the former disappearing almost entirely while the latter persists in emission throughout the photometric fade and into quiescent brightness. In the last few observations, the line widths narrow by $\sim 50\%$ , however, the line bases still extend to $\pm 100$ km/s, similar to the He I line widths. As shown in Figure 7, the 2021-11-28 spectra is notably blueshifted for both FeI at 5455.61 Å and FeII at 5316.62 Å which precedes a local photometric maximum.

### IV.3 Outflow Diagnostics

#### IV.3.1 Sodium and Potassium Lines

*Figure 8: Spectra for the NaD line centered at 5895.94 Å (top) and KI line centered at 7698.96 Å (bottom). The narrow absorption features around -29 and -5 km/s in the NaI D line, and the higher velocity (-29 km/s) narrow feature in the KI line maintain stable velocities across all epochs. The lower velocity absorption feature in KI shows a shift to slightly higher velocities (-2 to -4 km/s) as the star fades.*

The NaD and the KI doublet lines, while also tracing accretion [33] are frequently associated with winds in YSO spectra [13]. These features are illustrated in Figure 8.

Both the NaI D line centered at 5895.94 Å and the KI line centered at 7698.96 Å exhibit narrow blueshifted absorption components seen against the broader emission spectrum. The morphology is similar to that observed in the CaII lines. These absorption features have a deep low-velocity component and a shallower high velocity component. Both components are relatively stable in velocity across all epochs, but the absorption depths vary. The morphology of the line wings also varies, suggesting temporal changes in the structure of the accretion/wind. In the NaI D line, the lower velocity absorption component is at -5.3 km/s with a FWHM of 9.7 km/s measured from the first spectrum collected. The higher velocity component is at -29.1 km/s and is broader than the low-velocity component, with a FWHM of 19.3 km/s measured from the first spectrum collected. We measure no significant velocity shifts or broadening in the NaI D narrow absorption.

We also note that the narrow components in NaI D are absorbing against a broader emission component that is asymmetric, peaking on the red side. In the KI line, by contrast, the narrow absorption components are seen against a broader emission peak that appears symmetric between the red and blue sides. Also unlike NaI D, the morphology of the KI narrow absorption components evolves slightly over time.

In the KI line, the lower velocity narrow absorption component line is initially at -1.8 km/s, but shifts to slightly higher velocities as the star fades with -3.7 km/s measured in the final spectra. Over the final three epochs, this lower velocity absorption component deepens and broadens, from FWHM of 5.4 km/s in the earlier spectra to 9.3 km/s in the final spectrum. We interpret this low-velocity feature as transitioning from tracing only wind absorption, to also revealing the zero-velocity stellar photospheric absorption line. This behavior is similar to that of Li I, where a decline in the continuum flux over time allows the underlying photospheric absorption to emerge. Meanwhile, the higher velocity narrow absorption component is blueshifted to -28.6 km/s across all epochs. This feature broadens only slightly as the star fades to a FWHM of 6.5 km/s measured from the final spectrum.

Due to the complex structure of the lines, we did not compute equivalent width measurements.

#### IV.3.2 Forbidden Lines

Optical forbidden lines of [O I] and [S II] trace outflowing gas in young stars, with the lines formed in the shock interaction of accretion-driven jets and gas in the ambient environment.

Both of these lines are doublets, but we present here only the stronger line in each case, specifically the [OI] 6300.30 Å line (6363 Å exhibits the same morphology only weaker, with the expected 3:1 ratio), and the [SII] 6730.82 Å line (6716 Å shows the same morphology, but is weaker with 2:1 ratio). We also note that V347 Aur has weak [CaII] 7291.47 and 7323.89 Å emission, but we do not discuss these lines any further.

The time series of [OI] and [SII] profiles is shown in Figure 9. Both species exhibit distinct low-velocity and high-velocity components, with all peaks entirely blueshifted. As the star fades, both peaks in both species become more sharply peaked and narrower.

The [OI] profile has two components of comparable strength. The line-to-continuum intensity of the higher velocity component reaches a peak 0.92 times that of the lower velocity component in the 2022-02-16 (last) spectrum. The high-velocity component is centered at $-100$ km/s and the low-velocity component near $-8$ km/s. Broad high-velocity wings extend out to $+90$ km/s and $-200$ km/s. The implied centroid for the broad part of the low-velocity component would thus be about $-55$ km/s, consistent with formation in a turbulent wind. The overall morphology of the [OI] line profile, with a broad shoulder between the low-and high-velocity peaks which have comparable line-to-continuum strength, resembles the morphology seen in the source AS 353A [5]. These authors also present [OI] FWHM values as a function of the [OI] centroid velocities for their sample. Objects with the most blueshifted centroids tend to have the broadest high velocity component, while less blueshifted low-velocity components span a wide range of FWHM values, from comparably broad to narrower than the high-velocity component population. This is broadly consistent with what we observe in V347 Aur, where the peak of the high velocity component is broader than the peak of the low-velocity component by a factor of 1.76 (measured from the 2022-02-16 spectrum), though the base of the low velocity component is comparably broad to that of the high velocity component.

The [SII] profile, by contrast, exhibits two entirely blueshifted components at $-105$ km/s and another at $-25$ km/s. The higher velocity component is always larger than the lower velocity component, with the relative line-to-continuum intensity between the two components peaking at 1.3 in the 2022-02-16 spectrum. Furthermore, there is no obvious broader element in the low-velocity component, and specifically no redshifted emission as we observe in the [OI] line.

Due to the complex structure of the forbidden lines, we did not compute equivalent width measurements.
