## V Discussion

We have analyzed a sequence of high dispersion optical spectra for the quasi-periodic outbursting young stellar object V347 Aur, taken during the decline phase of a recent brightening event (Figure 1). The multi-epoch dataset shows systematic change in spectral line strength and morphology that can be correlated with the photometric brightness of the source. In this section we discuss the accretion diagnostics, then the outflow and wind diagnostics, and finally the implications of our results.

### V.1 Accretion Continuum and Line Emission

During the earlier epochs of our spectroscopic data set, when the source was brighter, photospheric absorption features including TiO and Li I are strongly veiled and nearly undetectable. These features re-emerge during quiescence, when the excess continuum emission is reduced, allowing the underlying photospheric spectrum to be revealed (Figures 2 and 3). The observed trend is consistent with a scenario in which accretion is stronger during the earlier epochs, when the source is near its peak brightness, and excess continuum emission from hot gas veils the underlying photospheric spectrum, filling in absorption features. As the accretion rate drops and the source fades, the veiling diminishes, and the intrinsic absorption features become more detectable.

Balmer line emission is a long-standing tracer of the accretion flow [33]. As V347 Aur fades, the Balmer lines generally decrease in strength and the line profiles appear sharper and more structured (Figure 4).

The Balmer profiles also undergo morphological evolution. Early spectra are asymmetric towards the red side, or have double peaked profiles preferentially in the red, while later epochs show enhanced blue-side emission and the development of a more complex blueshifted emission. This may reflect early emission dominated by magnetospheric accretion and post-shock regions and later, reduced veiling allows us to see blueshifted wind emission and multiple velocity components.

Broad Ca II emission is also generally attributed to the magnetospheric accretion flow [29]. In V347 Aur, the Ca II emission profiles display two prominent components, a redshifted and a blueshifted peak, whose relative strengths vary across epochs and between the two lines (Figure 5). The Ca II 3968.47 Å line consistently exhibits a stronger blueshifted component than redshifted component. In contrast, the Ca II 3933.66 Å line shows the opposite behavior at early epochs, with the redshifted component dominating, until the 2022-01-19 epoch, when this trend reverses. Although these lines share a lower level, the upper level of the K (3933.66 Å) line is slightly higher than the upper level of the H (3968.47 Å) line, the latter of which can have contamination from H $\epsilon$ at 3971.20 Å. The alternating dominance between redshifted and blueshifted emission components is suggestive of a magnetospheric accretion geometry where the emitting region co-rotates with the star. As the system rotates, the orientation of the accretion funnels and associated emitting regions changes relative to the observer, leading to variations in the line of sight velocities. At times, emission from material moving toward the observer becomes more prominent, producing stronger blueshifted components, while at others, emission from receding material dominates, enhancing the redshifted side of the profile. In addition, accretion flows are not perfectly smooth. Localized high density regions or clumping within the funnel flows could further contribute to the relative contributions of the redshifted and blueshifted components, contributing to the observed asymmetries. However, our observations are sparse relative to the $\sim 4.1$ day rotation period [11]; thus we cannot confirm this interpretation.

He I emission [13, 25] is formed both in the accretion funnel flows and in the outflowing wind. The accretion shock forms the narrow component (NC) in the post-shock gas at the footprint of the accretion column, and the outflowing wind contributes the wide range of velocities in the broad component (BC), as described in [7, 29]. In V347 Aur, the He I veiling-corrected equivalent widths decrease as the star fades (Figure 6). Additionally, the lines do not display similar behavior between their NC and BC. The BC is traditionally found to vary in sync with other accretion tracers, such as the veiling [8] or the Balmer lines [45]; however, we do not see this trend in our spectra. The NC has been found to show notable amplitude variations [45]; this is consistent with our spectra.

We infer that as the star fades, the He I emission becomes less dominated by accretion and increasingly influenced by blueshifted material in the wind, shifting the line peaks towards the blue.

### V.2 Wind and Outflow Diagnostics

In H $\alpha$ , there is blueshifted absorption superimposed on the broad emission profile, seen at different velocities over the different spectral epochs. We call attention to the feature at -40 km/s in the 2022-01-19 epoch, and note that similar features are apparent at other epochs. This morphology could be a sign of mass outflow in the form of a wind [25]. [22] suggest that the blueshifted absorption in Balmer lines arises in a low-density, optically thin wind, which they speculate originates from outside the magnetosphere, whereas the majority of the line emission originates in the infalling flow. This is consistent with wind models from [27], where blueshifted absorption components are caused by the conical-shell wind.

$H\alpha$ has a higher optical depth than $H\gamma$ and $H\delta$ , which may explain why the higher Balmer lines retain clearer signatures of the underlying emission structure. Calvet and Hartmann [9] produced central and low-velocity narrow absorption against broad emission profiles for Balmer lines in magnetospheric infall/accretion models, when they are viewed at certain viewing geometries i.e. inclinations. Here we note that [11] report inclination $i=26\pm 5$ deg for V347 Aur based on their measured projected rotational velocity and an inferred stellar radius. However, the features we see occur over a range of velocities, that are different at different epochs. It is also possible that the variable location of the narrow absorption is a consequence of the complex line radiative transfer in a rotating, accreting magnetosphere.

Besides the narrow blueshifted features in H $\alpha$ that are time-variable, V347 Aur also exhibits persistent, narrow, blueshifted absorption lines that are seen against the broad emission profiles in several other species: CaII, NaI D, and KI (Figures 5 and 8). This also nominally points to self-absorption by cooler gas within the winds.

It should be noted that there is interstellar contribution to the absorption in these Ca II, NaI D, and KI lines. NaI D and KI column densities are usually well-correlated [43, e.g.] with CaII tracing higher temperature gas along the line of sight. For a sample of YSOs in Taurus, Pascucci et al. [35] argued that narrow low-velocity absorptions in NaI D and KI are neither circumstellar nor from local (to the sun) interstellar matter, but rather are formed in the cooler larger-scale Taurus molecular cloud. In V347 Aur, the narrow absorption components have observed FWHM values ranging up to 19.3 km/s. These widths can be compared to values observed in the local ISM, which out to 300 pc do not exceed FWHM=5.8 km/s ( $b=3.5$ km/s) as reported by [42]. The relatively broad width of these narrow absorption components indicates that they cannot solely be attributed to the interstellar medium, supporting the self-absorption interpretation.

The narrow absorption components are largely stable in velocity over time, indicating a steadier wind geometry with the absorbers likely tracing gas further from the star, where velocities have reached a roughly constant value. In CaII, two persistent absorption components are present for both the H and K transitions. The low-velocity components are at about -8 km/s and the high-velocity components are at about -30.5 km/s. NaI D likewise exhibits two narrow absorption components, at -5.3 km/s and -29.1 km/s, which are similar velocities to the CaII H and K lines. For both CaII and NaI D, these velocities are fixed across epochs. In K I, the lower velocity component shifts to slightly higher velocities (from -1.8 to -3.7 km/s) as the star fades, but the higher velocity component at -28.6 km/s is similarly stable. With the exception of the low-velocity KI feature, the consistent absorption velocities across epochs favor a steadier wind geometry, rather than a “dynamic” wind.

While the absorption components show some correspondence across species – particularly the component near -29 km/s, their velocities are not identical between line species, particularly the lower velocity features. This behavior implies different formation locations in the wind. In this scenario, CaII, with an ionization potential of 11.9 eV, could persist under denser conditions closer to the wind base, while NaI and KI, with lower ionization potentials (5.14 eV and 4.34 eV respectively), could trace cooler material further out as they cannot survive as neutrals close to the host star. Additionally, the CaII absorption lines are at higher velocities than NaI D and KI, so may be tracing the wind closer to the star than further out, when it has slowed down.

The lowest-velocity KI absorption component shifts slightly towards higher velocities, deepens, and broadens, suggesting a transition from tracing wind absorption to revealing the underlying stellar photospheric line as continuum veiling declines. This is similar to the behavior of the Li I line, where a decline in continuum veiling over time allows the underlying photospheric absorption to emerge. Thus, not all low-velocity absorption necessarily originates in the outflow.

The existence of multiple narrow absorption components in these species is reminiscent of RU Lup, which displays narrow absorption components in the broad emission lines of CaII H and K and NaI D [1]. Similar to V347 Aur, the intensities and line profiles of these lines stay relatively constant, independent of the brightness variations of the star. [19] conclude that this behavior in RU Lup indicates that the gas flow must originate far out from the star and enclose the stellar wind. Additionally, they concluded that the blueshifted absorption spectrum could be related to irregularities such as pockets or shells of higher density in the disk wind. This is consistent with our observations of multiple narrow absorption components that all reside at similar velocities, yet differ slightly between lines.

The [O I] and [S II] forbidden lines are widely used diagnostics of outflowing gas in young stellar objects [14, 18]. High-velocity components are generally interpreted as originating in a fast outflow or jet, while low-velocity components are attributed to an MHD wind. In V347 Aur, these lines are consistently blueshifted (Figure 9), consistent with the outflow geometry in which the receding (redshifted) component is at least partially obscured by the disk.

There is no noticeable change in the locations of the peaks, indicating that the jet persists at a similar velocity, while the observed line strengths relative to continuum are affected by changes in the accretion rate. The persistent line morphology suggests a stable outflow geometry. However as the star fades, both peaks in both species become narrower and more sharply peaked, suggesting a transition to a less turbulent wind.

The [OI] line exhibits broad high-velocity wings on both the redshifted and blueshifted sides. In contrast, the [SII] line lacks a redshifted emission wing. The differing behavior between [OI] and [SII] can be interpreted in terms of line critical densities, and thus the regions of the outflow they trace. The [OI] line has a higher critical density than [SII], thus the [OI] transition is able to occur in dense gas that is closer to the star, including the base of the jet and inner disk wind. In these regions, some emission from the receding side of the flow may remain visible, producing the observed redshifted wing. The [SII] transition has a lower critical density, thus it is not able to occur in regions as dense as the [OI] transition, and must occur further out along the outflow, where the receding side is more effectively hidden by the disk or other circumstellar material. As a result, the redshifted emission may be suppressed in [SII] – as we observe.

Our observations are consistent with previous work demonstrating that [OI] traces both a dense inner wind and the base of a jet, while [SII] probes a lower density and more extended portion of the jet, with the disk geometry such that the redshifted component of the jet is blocked.

### V.3 The Binary-Induced Pulsed Accretion Model for V347 Aur

As discussed in detail by Dahm and Hillenbrand [10] who proposed it, and by Donati et al. [11] who confirmed it, a viable model for the photometric and spectroscopic behavior of V347 Aur is an orbiting binary system in which a burst of accretion is dynamically induced near the periastron passage [3, 32]. Other well-studied examples of this phenomenon are: DQ Tau, UZ Tau E, and TWA 3. In these systems, the enhanced accretion is assumed to occur onto the primary. We note that our observations of V347 Aur do not spatially or spectrally resolve the binary.

[11] interpret their data in terms of the binary influencing the magnetic field. They speculate that pulsed accretion, driven by the companion’s periastron passages, enhances shearing in the convective layers of the star and amplifies the large-scale toroidal field, a process they describe as a “pulsed dynamo.” They also discuss that the system may host an inner disk cavity that could pump the observed orbital eccentricity of the companion, through interactions with the disk. They further propose that this eccentric orbit would, in turn, carve a deeper cavity over time. This process could explain the enhanced accretion episodes observed at periastron passage in both the photometric light curve and the corresponding signatures in the spectra.

Our measurements are of spectral line changes in V347 Aur as it recovers in brightness from a photometric outburst that is attributed to a temporarily increased accretion rate. The observations cover a time period of months during which the accretion rate declines by over an order of magnitude, and are the first to link the photometric and emission line behavior in this source. Our results can inform models of pulsed accretion in binary systems. They are also applicable to the more general area of accretion variability in young stellar objects.

## VI Summary

We have presented the results of time series optical spectroscopy at high dispersion obtained during the decay phase of an accretion burst in the young stellar object V347 Aur.

Our spectral dataset consists of eight epochs. We analyze the lines of Li I (6707.86 Å), H I (H $\alpha$ , H $\delta$ , H $\gamma$ ), HeI (5875.62 Å, 6678.15 Å), CaII (3968.47 Å, 3933.66 Å), FeI (5455.61 Å), FeII (5316.62 Å), KI (7698.96 Å), NaD 5895.94 Å), [OI] (6300.30 Å), and [SII] (6730.82 Å). We have measured line center shifts, line broadening, equivalent widths, and detailed the changes in line profile morphology.

As V347 Aur fades, photospheric absorption features deepen, consistent with a reduction in accretion driven continuum veiling. The broad emission lines all generally increase in their observed line-to-continuum strength as the source fades, but decrease in veiling-corrected equivalent width with the presumed decreasing accretion rate. The Balmer emission lines transition to a more blueshifted profile as the star fades, as do the HeI lines. The CaII line profiles show alternating dominance between redshifted and blueshifted components, which we interpret as the rotation of the system and changing viewing angles of the magnetospheric funnel flows. We also detect narrow, blueshifted absorption components in CaII, NaD, and KI that exhibit correlation with one another. Forbidden emission lines have multiple components and are consistently blueshifted and trace the kinematics of outflowing material. The [OI] emission likely originates from a denser, inner wind region, while the [SII] line probes lower density, more extended jet material. The absence of strong redshifted emission, particularly in [SII], is consistent with a disk geometry that partially obscures the receding side of the outflow.

In this paper we have mapped the changes in observed accretion and outflow diagnostics in a periodically outbursting YSO that experiences order-of-magnitude variations in its accretion rate on time scales of months. The V347 Aur system is a useful proxy both for the ubiquitous short-term accretion variability observed in YSOs, and for their long-term secular evolution.

# Gauge Boundary conditions to mitigate center-of-mass drift in BBH simulations

**Authors:** Dongze Sun Email: dzsun@caltech.edu Affiliation: Theoretical Astrophysics 350-17, California Institute of Technology, 1200 E California Boulevard, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA Sizheng Ma Affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo, ON N2L2Y5, Canada Mark A. Scheel Affiliation: Theoretical Astrophysics 350-17, California Institute of Technology, 1200 E California Boulevard, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA Saul A. Teukolsky Affiliation: Theoretical Astrophysics 350-17, California Institute of Technology, 1200 E California Boulevard, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA Affiliation: Cornell Center for Astrophysics and Planetary Science, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14853, USA

## Abstract

Long-term numerical relativity (NR) simulations of binary black hole (BBH) systems in the Spectral Einstein Code (SpEC) code exhibit an unexpected exponential drift of the center-of-mass (CoM) away from the simulation’s origin. In our work, we analyze this phenomenon and demonstrate that it is not a physical effect but rather a manifestation of a gauge artifact. The origin of this drift is the reflection of the gauge waves off the outer boundary of the computational domain. These reflections are introduced by inaccuracies in the gauge boundary condition, specifically, the application of the Sommerfeld condition to the time derivative of the gauge fields. Such an approach fails to completely suppress or correctly absorb the outgoing modes, thereby generating artificial feedback into the simulation. To mitigate this problem, we introduce a modified boundary condition that incorporates an explicit CoM correction source term designed to counteract the CoM motion. Our numerical experiments, performed with the SpEC code, reveal that this new boundary treatment reduces the CoM drift by several orders of magnitude compared to the standard implementation, and does not introduce any unwanted physical artifacts.

## I Introduction

Numerical relativity (NR) provides the most accurate solution for the dynamics and gravitational-wave emission of binary black holes (BBHs). The first stable BBH evolutions were obtained by Pretorius [37] in the generalized-harmonic formulation, followed soon after by the moving-puncture breakthroughs of Campanelli et al. [19] and Baker et al. [4]. These NR results play a crucial role in understanding the dynamics of these astrophysical phenomena, and the behavior of gravity in extreme regimes [1, 2, 3].

Despite major successes, long-duration NR simulations remain sensitive to how the artificial outer boundary is treated. In generalized-harmonic (GH) evolutions with the Spectral Einstein Code (SpEC) [45], an exponential drift of the BBH system’s coordinate center-of-mass (CoM) has been consistently observed [44]. Figure 1 illustrates this drift, which is a steadily increasing displacement of the CoM from the coordinate origin over time. It is unclear whether this boundary issue would occur for moving-puncture/BSSN codes; unlike SpEC, these codes generally place the boundary very far out so that it is causally disconnected over the simulation time [36, 25, 24, 30].

To uncover the cause of this spurious CoM behavior, Ref. [44] manipulated the outer boundary radius and observed that the exponential growth rate, denoted by $\sigma$ , decreases monotonically with increasing boundary distance as $\sigma\propto 1/R^{1.45}$ . This sensitivity to the boundary location strongly indicates that the drift is related to a coupling between the evolving fields and the computational boundary. This effect makes it infeasible to conduct long-term NR simulations with small outer boundary radii. To prevent the drift from affecting the simulation and waveform extraction, the outer boundary is typically set at radii on the order of $10^{3}\,M$ [14], where $M$ is the total mass of the system. Although such large boundaries mitigate the drift, they also come with an increase in computational expense. Therefore, it is imperative to thoroughly investigate and address this issue to enable more efficient long-term NR simulations.

In our study, we probe this effect and find that the CoM drift is predominantly a gauge effect arising from the reflection of gauge waves off the outer boundary. These reflections are caused by the imperfect non-reflective Sommerfeld boundary condition applied to the time derivative of the gauge variables. Essentially, while the Sommerfeld condition is non-reflective for $l=0$ outgoing radiation modes, any nonzero displacement of the CoM will generate higher-order outgoing radiation modes that can be reflected by the Sommerfeld condition. These reflected waves caused by the Sommerfeld condition then propel the CoM with exponential acceleration. Since the Sommerfeld condition is only imposed on the gauge degrees of freedom of the fields, the physical CoM defined from global Poincaré charges [21, 22, 31] is not affected and does not exhibit exponential drift, as we will show in Sec. II.

Motivated by these insights, we propose an improved boundary treatment that mitigates the CoM drift. We add an additional CoM correction source term to the boundary condition. This term is formulated to effectively dampen the CoM velocity or realign the CoM with the coordinate origin. Numerical tests using our modified boundary condition demonstrate a significant reduction in the drift amplitude, by several orders of magnitude relative to the original setup. Thus, our modification not only clarifies the origin of the CoM drift but also provides a practical solution for performing long-term BBH simulations with smaller outer boundary radii and reduced computational cost.

In this paper, we use lower-case Latin indices from the beginning of the alphabet to denote four-dimensional spacetime quantities, whereas lower-case Latin indices from the middle of the alphabet are spatial. The coordinate CoM is defined using the Newtonian formula as

$$ \bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}=\frac{m_{1}\bm{\mathrm{r_{1}}}+m_{2}\bm{\mathrm{r_{2}}}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}, $$

where $\bm{\mathrm{r_{1}}}$ and $\bm{\mathrm{r_{2}}}$ are the coordinates of the center of the two black holes, which are defined as the surface-area weighted average of the location of the apparent horizons [14].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we show that the CoM drift is a gauge effect by inspecting the physical charges. In Sec. III, we review the Sommerfeld gauge boundary condition that is used in SpEC, and we discuss why this boundary condition leads to the exponential drift of the CoM. In Sec. IV, we derive the equation of motion of the CoM under given gauge boundary conditions. Following this, we present the new boundary conditions that significantly damp the CoM drift in Sec. V. And we show that the gauge boundary conditions do not affect the resulting gauge-fixed waveform in Sec. VI. In Sec. VII, we discuss the potential of using higher-order boundary conditions, gauge constraint damping boundary condition, NR-post-Minkowskian matching, or Cauchy-Characteristic matching (CCM) as potential alternative solutions to address the CoM drift. In Sec. VIII, we provide a few closing remarks. The BBH simulations used in this paper are performed by the SpEC code [45].

## II CoM drift as a gauge effect

To identify whether the CoM drift is a physical or gauge effect, we inspect the Poincaré charges that are associated with the global conserved physical quantities. These charges are gauge-invariant up to the well-understood Bondi-van der Burg-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) group freedom [39, 40, 13]. We will address the BMS frame ambiguity in Sec. VI. The Poincaré charges are given by the integral of the Bondi mass aspect $m_{\text{B}}$ , the Lorentz aspect $N$ , and the energy moment aspect $E$ over the celestial two-sphere (future null infinity $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ from the source) [13]. These functions are given in the Moreschi-Boyle convention [17, 31, 32] using the Bondi-Sachs coordinates $\{u,r,\theta^{A}\}$ as

$$ \displaystyle m_{\text{B}}(u,\theta^{A}) \displaystyle\equiv-\mathrm{Re}\left[\Psi_{2}+\sigma\dot{\bar{\sigma}}\right], \displaystyle N(u,\theta^{A}) \displaystyle\equiv-\left(\Psi_{1}+\sigma\eth\bar{\sigma}+u\eth m+\frac{1}{2}\eth(\sigma\bar{\sigma})\right), \displaystyle E(u,\theta^{A}) \displaystyle\equiv N+u\eth m \displaystyle=-\left(\Psi_{1}+\sigma\eth\bar{\sigma}+\frac{1}{2}\eth(\sigma\bar{\sigma})\right). $$

Here $\Psi_{i}$ are the Weyl scalars, $\sigma$ is the Newman-Penrose shear, and an overbar represents complex conjugation. For a quantity $\eta$ of spin weight $s$ , the spin-weight raising operator $\eth$ can be written as [35, 16]

$$ \eth\eta=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\sin\theta)^{s}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}+\frac{i}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}\right)\left((\sin\theta)^{-s}\eta\right). $$

With these functions defined at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ , we then have the energy–momentum charge and complex dipole moment defined as

$$ \displaystyle P^{a} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}n^{a}m_{\text{B}}d\Omega, \displaystyle D^{a}+iJ^{a} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathscr{I}^{+}}\bar{\eth}n^{a}Ed\Omega, $$

where $n^{a}=\left(1,\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\cos\phi,\cos\theta\right)$ . Here the real part $D$ defines the gauge-independent mass dipole, and the imaginary part $J$ defines the angular momentum.

A gauge-independent measurement of the CoM displacement, i.e., the CoM charge, can be defined as the mass dipole $D$ scaled by the total energy $P^{0}$ [21, 22, 31]:

$$ G^{i}\equiv\frac{D^{i}}{P^{0}}. $$

To carry out this check, we use Cauchy-characteristic evolution (CCE) to extract the Weyl scalars and $\sigma$ at $\mathscr{I}^{+}$ [34, 33]. The Cauchy evolution parts are performed using the SpEC code [45], and the CCE computations are performed using the SpECTRE Code [20]. CCE uses a worldtube from the Cauchy evolution of the Einstein field equations as the inner boundary to a characteristic evolution on a null foliation. The gravitational information is evolved to future null infinity, so one can extract Weyl scalars there unambiguously from any Cauchy evolution.

Fig. 2 shows the evolution of CoM coordinates alongside the corresponding CoM charges of an equal-mass and non-spinning system. The CoM charges are computed using the scri package [15]. The CoM charges in each direction shown in the lower panel are considerably smaller than the corresponding CoM coordinates shown in the upper panel, and they do not exhibit exponential growth. This is strong evidence that the exponential CoM drift primarily arises as a gauge effect caused by inaccuracies in the gauge boundary conditions, rather than a genuine physical motion.

## III Sommerfeld boundary condition

In this section, we first review the gauge boundary condition used in the SpEC code, and then use a propagating scalar wave as a toy model to show how reflections can be generated by this boundary condition.

### III.1 Gauge boundary condition in SpEC

The gauge boundary condition used in SpEC is the Sommerfeld non-reflective boundary condition [41, 38]. The Sommerfeld boundary condition acts on a general propagating tensor wave $\Psi$ as

$$ L\Psi\doteq 0, $$

where

$$ L=\partial_{t}+\partial_{r}+\frac{1}{r}, $$

and $\doteq$ denotes equality at the boundary.

For gravitational waves, the spacetime metric can be approximately decomposed as a background part $g_{ab}^{\text{(B)}}$ that changes “adiabatically”, and a propagating wave part $h_{ab}$ :

$$ g_{ab}=g_{ab}^{\text{(B)}}+h_{ab}. $$

The Sommerfeld boundary condition should then act like

$$ Lh_{ab}\doteq 0. $$

The use of approximations for $g_{ab}^{\text{(B)}}$ may introduce inaccuracies in the boundary condition, leading to junk reflections within the simulation domain. To address this issue, we can further refine the boundary condition by taking a time derivative, thus removing the ambiguity in $g_{ab}^{\text{(B)}}$ , resulting in

$$ \partial_{t}\left(Lg_{ab}\right)\doteq 0. $$

In SpEC, the Einstein equations are solved using the generalized harmonic (GH) formalism, with the gauge condition given by

$$ \nabla^{c}\nabla_{c}x^{a}=H^{a}, $$

where $H^{a}$ are the gauge source functions. In the GH formalism, the Einstein equations can be written in first-order form [26] by introducing the derivatives of $g_{ab}$ as additional variables $\Phi_{iab}\equiv\partial_{i}g_{ab}$ and $\Pi_{ab}\equiv-t^{c}\partial_{c}g_{ab}$ , where $t^{c}$ is the future directed unit normal to the $t=\text{constant}$ hypersurfaces. The gauge boundary condition is imposed on the incoming characteristic field, given by

$$ u_{ab}^{1-}=\Pi_{ab}-n^{i}\Phi_{iab}-\gamma_{2}g_{ab}, $$

where $n^{i}$ is the outward-pointing spatial normal vector to the outer boundary, and $\gamma_{2}$ is introduced to damp the constraint violation $\partial_{i}g_{ab}-\Phi_{iab}$ . The ingoing and outgoing null vectors are given by $k^{a}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(t^{a}-n^{a}\right)$ and $l^{a}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(t^{a}+n^{a}\right)$ . In this notation, if we assume the background metric to be either constant or changes “adiabatically”, i.e., $\partial_{t}g_{ab}^{\text{B}}\sim\frac{v}{c}\partial_{t}h_{ab}$ , where $v$ is the coordinate velocity of the BH and $v/c\ll 1$ , and $h_{ab}$ is a spherical wave, then the Sommerfeld gauge boundary condition reads approximately as

$$ P^{\text{G}cd}_{ab}d_{t}\left[u_{cd}^{1-}+\left(\gamma_{2}-\frac{1}{r}\right)g_{cd}\right]\doteq 0. $$

Here $P^{\text{G}cd}_{ab}=\left[k_{a}k_{b}l^{(c}+k_{a}\delta_{b}^{(c}+k_{b}\delta_{a}^{(c}\right]l^{d)}$ is the projection operator that removes the four constraint-preserving degrees of freedom corresponding to the incoming constraint fields and two physical degrees of freedom that correspond to backscattered gravitational waves. This leaves four degrees of freedom that correspond to the gauge part of the field, which determine the lapse and shift (see [38] for more details). Here $d_{t}u$ is the incoming characteristic projection of $\partial_{t}u$ , as defined in Ref. [26]: If the fundamental fields are $u^{\alpha}$ and the characteristic fields are $u^{\hat{\alpha}}\equiv e^{\hat{\alpha}}{}_{\beta}u^{\beta}$ where Greek letters label each field and $e^{\hat{\alpha}}{}_{\beta}$ are the characteristic eigenvectors, then $d_{t}u^{\hat{\alpha}}\equiv e^{\hat{\alpha}}{}_{\beta}\partial_{t}u^{\beta}$ .

### III.2 Reflection from the boundary condition

To understand how the CoM drift is coupled with the outer boundary condition, we first consider a scalar wave in 3-dimensional flat space as a toy model:

$$ \psi_{\ell mk}(r,\theta,\phi,t)=e^{ikt}\Big(h^{(1)}_{\ell}(k|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|)Y^{m}_{\ell}(\theta,\phi)\\
+\sum_{\ell^{\prime},m^{\prime}}\rho^{\ell}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}h^{(2)}_{\ell^{\prime}}(k|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|)Y^{m^{\prime}}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\theta,\phi)\Big), $$

where $h^{(1)},h^{(2)}$ are spherical Hankel functions that correspond to the outgoing and ingoing waves, $\rho^{\ell}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}$ are the reflection coefficients, and $\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}$ is the location of the source.

We impose the Sommerfeld boundary condition Eq. (6) on this scalar field, and calculate $\rho^{\ell}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}$ for $0\leq\ell\leq 3$ , $\ell^{\prime}=\ell$ and $m^{\prime}=0$ . In Fig. 3, we show the results as a function of the distance of the source from the origin, $r_{\text{s}}$ , normalized by the outer boundary radius $R$ . We can see that the Sommerfeld boundary condition is only perfectly non-reflective for the $\ell=0$ mode for a source located at the origin ( $r_{\text{s}}=0$ ). When the source is positioned away from the origin ( $r_{\text{s}}>0$ ), there will be mode mixing and the Sommerfeld boundary condition is not non-reflective anymore. As we shall show below in Sec. IV, this reflection of the gauge wave leads to the drift of the CoM observed in BBH simulations.

*Figure 3: Reflection coefficient $|\rho^{\ell}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}|$ for different $\ell$ . Given $m^{\prime}=0,\ell^{\prime}=\ell,k=1,t=0,\theta=\phi=0$ .*

This leads us to generalize the Sommerfeld boundary condition in Eq. (6) by introducing a parameter $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ . The radial coordinate $r$ is modified to $|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}|$ , in order to eliminate the reflections of $\ell\neq 0$ modes

$$ L(\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}})\psi\doteq 0, $$

where

$$ L(\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}})=\partial_{t}+\partial_{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}|}+\frac{1}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}|}. $$

$L(0)\psi\doteq 0$ corresponds to the original Sommerfeld boundary condition.

*Figure 4: Reflection coefficient $|\rho|$ for a spherical wave whose source is localized at $\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}/R=0.15$ , with $k=1,t=0,\theta=\phi=0$ .*

To show how the introduced parameter $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ works, we consider a spherical wave sourced at $\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}$ instead of the origin,

$$ \psi(\bm{\mathrm{r}},t)=\frac{1}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}\left(e^{ik(|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|-t)}+\rho e^{-ik(|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|+t)}\right), $$

which has nonzero $\ell$ modes with respect to the origin. In this case we can adjust the $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ parameter in Eq. (16) to shift the boundary condition with respect to the source, effectively eliminating reflected waves. Fig. 4 illustrates the reflection coefficient $\rho$ as a function of $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ . Notably, when $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}=\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}$ , the boundary condition becomes non-reflective, demonstrating its efficacy in preventing wave reflections.

## IV CoM dynamics

In this section we will derive the leading-order equation of motion for the CoM under the interaction with the outer boundary gauge reflection. The derivation will only focus on the leading-order effects.

*Figure 5: A schematic diagram showing the domain setup and symbols.*

We use the following notation: $\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}$ is the location of the CoM. $\bm{\mathrm{R}}$ is the field point on the outer boundary, and $\bm{\mathrm{x_{1}}}$ and $\bm{\mathrm{x_{2}}}$ are the locations of the black holes. We assume $\mathrm{r_{s}}\ll r_{12}=|\bm{\mathrm{x_{1}}}-\bm{\mathrm{x_{2}}}|\ll R$ , and $\mathrm{r_{s}}\ll 1/k$ , where $k$ is the wavenumber of the metric perturbation. The setup is shown in the schematic diagram in Fig. 5. The metric perturbation in the region near the outer boundary ( $r\sim R\gg r_{12}$ ) can be written as the summation of outgoing and ingoing waves

$$ h_{ab}(\bm{\mathrm{r}},t)=h_{ab}^{\text{outgoing}}(\bm{\mathrm{r}},t)+h_{ab}^{\text{ingoing}}(\bm{\mathrm{r}},t)\\
{}=\Big(f^{\text{out}}_{ab}(\theta,\phi)\frac{e^{ik|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}+f^{\text{in}}_{ab}(\theta,\phi)\sum_{\ell^{\prime}}\rho_{\ell^{\prime}}h_{\ell^{\prime}}^{(2)}\left(kr\right)\Big)e^{-ikt}\\
+O\left(\frac{1}{R^{2}}\right). $$

Near the outer boundary, the quantity $h_{\ell^{\prime}}^{(2)}\left(kr\right)$ behaves like $e^{-ikr}/r^{\ell+1}$ , so we will only focus on the dominant $\ell=0$ reflected mode. Substituting the Sommerfeld boundary condition Eq. (9), we obtain

$$ \rho_{0}=\frac{\hat{\bm{\mathrm{R}}}\cdot\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}}{2R^{2}}e^{2ikR}+O\left(\frac{r_{s}^{2}}{R^{2}}\right). $$

The ingoing perturbation is then given by

$$ h_{ab}^{\text{ingoing}}(\bm{\mathrm{r}},t)=f_{ab}^{\text{in}}(\theta,\phi)\frac{\hat{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}\cdot\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}}{2R^{2}}\frac{e^{ik(2R-r-t)}}{r}+O\left(\frac{r_{s}^{2}}{R^{3}}\right). $$

The momentum flux carried by a gravitational perturbation on the outer boundary is given by the integral of the Landau–Lifshitz pseudotensor on the outer boundary

$$ \frac{dP^{i}}{dt}=-\int_{r=R}t_{\text{LL}}^{ij}\hat{r}_{j}r^{2}d\Omega, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle t_{\text{LL}}^{ij}=\frac{1}{16\pi(-g)} \displaystyle\left[\partial_{a}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{ij}\right)\partial_{b}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{ab}\right)-\partial_{a}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{ia}\right)\partial_{b}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{jb}\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.+\frac{1}{2}g^{ij}g_{ab}\partial_{c}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{ad}\right)\partial_{d}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{bc}\right)+g_{ab}g^{cd}\partial_{c}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{ia}\right)\partial_{d}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{jb}\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.-\left(g^{ia}g_{bc}\partial_{d}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{jc}\right)\partial_{a}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{bd}\right)+g^{ja}g_{bc}\partial_{d}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{ic}\right)\partial_{a}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{bd}\right)\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.+\frac{1}{8}\left(2g^{ia}g^{jb}-g^{ij}g^{ab}\right)\left(2g_{cd}g_{ef}-g_{de}g_{cf}\right)\partial_{a}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{cf}\right)\partial_{b}\left(\sqrt{-g}g^{de}\right)\right] $$

is quadratic in the first derivatives of the metric. Using the decomposition

$$ g_{ab}=g^{\text{(B)}}_{ab}+h^{\text{outgoing}}_{ab}+h^{\text{ingoing}}_{ab}, $$

the terms in the outer boundary integral in Eq. (21) that involve only $g^{\text{(B)}}_{ab}$ and $h^{\text{outgoing}}_{ab}$ drop out, because they are even functions with respect to the source when time-averaged over orbits, while $\hat{r}$ is odd, therefore their product is odd and integrates to zero over the boundary. So the leading-order non-vanishing result of the integral Eq. (21) comes from terms involving the product of $\partial_{a}g^{\text{(B)}}_{bc}$ and $\partial_{a}h^{\text{ingoing}}_{bc}$ . The terms involving the product of $\partial_{a}h^{\text{outgoing}}_{bc}$ and $\partial_{a}h^{\text{ingoing}}_{bc}$ are on the order of $\mathcal{O}(h^{2})$ , so we will ignore them in the leading-order calculation.

In the region near the outer boundary ( $r\sim R\gg r_{12}$ ), the background metric can be described using the post-Newtonian (PN) approximation [10, 11]

$$ \displaystyle g^{\text{(B)}}_{00}= \displaystyle-1+\frac{2Gm_{1}}{c^{2}r_{1}}+O\left(\frac{1}{c^{4}}\right)+1\leftrightarrow 2, \displaystyle g^{\text{(B)}}_{0i}= \displaystyle-\frac{4m_{1}}{c^{3}r_{1}}v_{1}^{i}+O\left(\frac{1}{c^{5}}\right)+1\leftrightarrow 2, \displaystyle g^{\text{(B)}}_{ij}= \displaystyle\left(1+\frac{2Gm_{1}}{c^{2}r_{1}}\right)\delta_{ij}+O\left(\frac{1}{c^{4}}\right)+1\leftrightarrow 2. $$

So we have $\partial_{a}g^{\text{(B)}}_{bc}\sim 1/R^{2}+O(v/R^{2})$ . And from Eq. (20), we have $\partial_{a}h^{\text{ingoing}}_{bc}\sim(\hat{\bm{\mathrm{R}}}\cdot r_{\text{s}})/R^{3}+O(r_{\text{s}}^{2}/R^{4})$ . Thus Eq. (21) gives $dP^{i}/dt\sim r_{\text{s}}^{i}/R^{3}$ at leading order. This leads us to the CoM equation of motion:

$$ \ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}(t)}-\frac{a}{R^{3}}\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}(t_{\text{ret}})}=0, $$

where $a$ is a dimensionless coefficient that collects the numerical factors from the leading-order evaluation of the outer boundary Landau-Lifshitz momentum flux, after keeping only the dominant $\partial g^{\text{(B)}}\partial h^{\text{ingoing}}$ contribution. Here, the momentum flux takes the value at a retarded time $t_{\text{ret}}\approx t-2R$ . For $t\gg R$ , the solution is given by

$$ \bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}(t)=\bm{\mathrm{A}}\exp\left(\frac{\sqrt{a}}{R^{3/2}}t\right). $$

The solution with a positive $a$ is consistent with [44], whose results showed the exponential growth rate $\sigma\propto R^{-1.45}$ , as shown in Fig. 1. In this leading order model the binary parameters primarily set the magnitude of the flux rather than its parity structure, so we do not expect the sign of the coefficient $a$ to change with binary parameters.

We emphasize that the mechanism underlying Eq. (25) requires the outer boundary to be causally connected with the source (i.e., that reflected gauge perturbations can return on a timescale $\sim 2R$ ). If instead the outer boundary is placed sufficiently far out that the evolution time satisfies $t_{\rm evol}\lesssim 2R$ , the feedback loop is effectively absent.

## V Modified boundary conditions

Having understood how the Sommerfeld boundary condition in Eq. (15) leads to exponential drift of the CoM, we now use Eq. (16) to modify the boundary condition to control the gauge reflection and the CoM drift. The parameter $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ is introduced as a source term in the boundary condition. Following the derivation in Sec. IV, we obtain the equation of motion for the CoM under Eq. (16)

$$ \ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}(t)}+\frac{a}{R^{3}}\left(\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\bm{0}}-\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}\right)_{(t_{\text{ret}})}=0. $$

For $t\gg R$ , the second term can be linearly expanded as

$$ \ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}-\frac{2b}{R^{2}}\left(\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{0}}-\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}\right)+\frac{a}{R^{3}}\left(\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}-\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}\right)=0, $$

where $b=(t-t_{\text{ret}})/(2R)$ .

We approximately treat $b$ as a constant parameter, given that the location of the outer boundary doesn’t change significantly during the simulation, i.e., $\Delta R/R\ll 1$ . Then we can treat the CoM coordinate quantities (i.e., $\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}$ , $\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}$ and $\ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}$ ) as measured at the time when the boundary condition is imposed, rather than at the retarded time.

One possible approach to control the drift is to allow the auxiliary parameter $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ above to depend on $\bm{\mathrm{r_{\text{s}}}}$ , $\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}$ and $t$ in a way that ensures the solution to Eq. (28) does not exhibit exponential growth. In the following, we consider two specific forms of such dependence.

#### V.0.1 Example 1

We take a simple case as an example. Consider $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}=\lambda\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}$ , where $\lambda$ is a free parameter. Substituting into the CoM equation of motion Eq. (28), we get

$$ \ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}-2\sigma\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}+\omega^{2}\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}=0, $$

where

$$ \sigma=b\frac{(\lambda-1)}{R^{2}},\quad\omega=\sqrt{a}\frac{(\lambda-1)^{1/2}}{R^{1.5}}. $$

For the limit $R\gg r_{\text{s}}$ and $t\gg 1$ , the equation gives

$$ \bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\bm{\mathrm{A}}e^{|\omega|t}&(\lambda<1),\\
\bm{\mathrm{A}}e^{\sigma t}\sin\left(\omega t+\phi_{0}\right)&(\lambda>1).\end{array}\right. $$

In terms of the incoming characteristic field, the boundary condition Eq. (16) reads

$$ \displaystyle P_{ab}^{\mathrm{G}cd}d_{t} \displaystyle\left[u_{cd}^{1-}+\left(n^{i}-\frac{r^{i}-\lambda r_{\text{s}}^{i}}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}\right)\Phi_{icd}\right. \displaystyle+\left.\left(\gamma_{2}-\frac{1}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\lambda\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}\right)g_{cd}\right]\doteq 0. $$

*Figure 6: The green and blue lines are the results for $R=100\,M,\lambda=5$ and $R=200\,M,\lambda=80$ , respectively, under gauge boundary condition Eq. (32). The wider gray lines are there fits. The system is equal-mass and non-spinning. The initial separation is $19\,M$ and the merger time is around $11000\,M$ .*

To test the model, we perform simulations of equal-mass and non-spinning system with different outer boundary radii $R$ and free parameter $\lambda$ . The initial separation is $19\,M$ and the merger time is around $11000\,M$ . The simulation results exhibit strong agreement with the model fitting based on Eq. (31), as shown in Figure 6. By fitting the growth rate $\sigma$ and frequency $\omega$ from Eq. (30) and (31) to the NR results for different $\lambda$ , we obtain the parameters $a=0.54$ and $b=0.64$ , which are independent of $\lambda$ . The parameter $b$ is greater than $a$ due to the GR time lag.

*Figure 7: Different results with similar $(\lambda-1)/R^{2}$ ratio under gauge boundary condition Eq. (32). The system is equal-mass and non-spinning. The initial separation is $19\,M$ and the merger time is around $11000\,M$ .*

To further test this model, we consider the growth rate $\sigma=0.64(\lambda-1)/R^{2}$ . According to this formulation, when $(\lambda-1)\sim R^{2}$ , the growth rate is expected to be independent of $R$ . We plot the CoM drift for different $R$ and $\lambda$ in Fig. 7. The observed results indeed agree with the anticipated behavior.

Eq. (31) shows that the growth rate of the solution is always positive, regardless of the value of the free parameter $\lambda$ . One way to decelerate the CoM is to introduce an additional term involving $\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}$ in the equation of motion, Eq. (29), to act as a damping term.

To do this, we introduce an additional velocity term to Eq. (16):

$$ L(\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}},\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}},\mu)=\partial_{t}+\partial_{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}|}+\frac{1}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}|}+\mu\bm{\mathrm{n}}\cdot\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}, $$

where $\bm{\mathrm{n}}$ represents the outward-pointing normal vector to the outer boundary, and $\mu$ is a parameter. With this modification, the boundary condition, expressed in terms of the incoming characteristic field, becomes:

$$ \displaystyle P_{ab}^{\mathrm{G}cd}d_{t} \displaystyle\left[u_{cd}^{1-}+\left(n^{i}-\frac{r^{i}-\lambda r_{\text{s}}^{i}}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\lambda\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}\right)\Phi_{icd}\right. \displaystyle+\left.\left(\gamma_{2}-\frac{1}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\lambda\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}\right)g_{cd}-\mu\frac{r^{i}-r_{\mathrm{s}}^{i}}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\lambda\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}|}\dot{r}_{\mathrm{s}}^{i}\right]\doteq 0. $$

Here $r_{s}$ and its time derivative are evaluated at the same coordinate time that the boundary condition is imposed. The post-Newtonian equation of motion of the CoM under this new boundary condition is then

$$ \left(1-2b\mu R\right)\ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}+\left(\mu-2\sigma\right)\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}+\omega^{2}\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}=0, $$

where $b$ is the dimensionless retarded time parameter introduced in Eq. (28). For this equation to exhibit damping behavior, the parameter $\mu$ must satisfy the following conditions:

$$ \left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}&\left(\mu-2\sigma\right)^{2}<4\omega^{2}(1-2b\mu R),\\
&2\sigma<\mu<\frac{1}{2bR}.\end{array}\right. $$

As a good choice, we can set

$$ \mu\equiv\omega+2\sigma. $$

*Figure 8: CoM drift and velocity under the gauge boundary condition Eq. (34) with $\lambda=1+(R/100)^{2}$ . The upper panel shows the CoM drift and the lower panel shows the CoM velocities. The black curves are the results obtained using the original Sommerfeld boundary condition, and the other curves are results with the new boundary condition for $R=100M,200M$ and $400M$ . The system is equal-mass and non-spinning. The initial separation is $19\,M$ and the merger time is around $11000\,M$ .*

Now the only remaining free parameter is $\lambda$ . As discussed in Sec. IV, we can set $(\lambda-1)\sim R^{2}$ so that the growth or damping rate becomes independent of the outer boundary radius. For $(\lambda-1)=(R/100)^{2}$ , the corresponding results are displayed in Fig. 8. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the modified boundary condition in damping the CoM drift.

An alternative way to introduce CoM damping for Eq. (29) without introducing an additional damping term like Eq. (33) is to use $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ in the boundary condition only when the CoM is accelerating. Namely,

$$ \bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\lambda\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}&(\ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}\cdot\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}\geq 0),\\
0&(\ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}\cdot\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}<0).\end{array}\right. $$

The result for this approach is shown in Fig. 9, where we increased the initial separation to $29\,M$ and the merger time to around $50000\,M$ to show the long term behavior, since the oscillation time scale is longer than the previous cases. This approach is more robust than Eq. (33) because it has fewer parameters.

The black curves are the results obtained using the original Sommerfeld boundary condition, and other curves are results under the new boundary condition for $R=200M,400M$ and $800M$ . #### V.0.2 Example 2

*Figure 10: CoM drift and velocity under gauge boundary condition Eq. (39) with $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}=\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}+\eta R\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}$ , where $\eta=R/4$ . The upper panel shows the CoM drift and the lower panel shows the CoM velocities. The black curves are the results obtained using the original Sommerfeld boundary condition, and the other curves are results under the new boundary condition for $R=200M,400M$ and $800M$ . The system is equal-mass and non-spinning. The initial separation is $29\,M$ and the merger time is around $50000\,M$ .*

Now we consider $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}=\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}+\eta R\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}$ , where $\eta$ is a free parameter. The boundary condition expressed in terms of the incoming characteristic field then reads

$$ \displaystyle P_{ab}^{\mathrm{G}cd}d_{t} \displaystyle\left[u_{cd}^{1-}+\left(n^{i}-\frac{r^{i}-r_{\text{s}}^{i}-\eta R\dot{r}_{\mathrm{s}}^{i}}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}-\eta R\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}|}\right)\Phi_{icd}\right. \displaystyle+\left.\left(\gamma_{2}-\frac{1}{|\bm{\mathrm{r}}-\bm{\mathrm{r_{s}}}-\eta R\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}|}\right)g_{cd}\right]\doteq 0. $$

Then the CoM equation of motion Eq. (28) becomes

$$ \alpha\ddot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\text{s}}+\beta\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}=0, $$

where

$$ \alpha=1-\frac{2b\eta}{R},\quad\beta=\frac{a\eta}{R^{2}}. $$

The equation gives

$$ \bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}=\bm{\mathrm{c_{1}}}-\bm{\mathrm{c_{2}}}e^{-\alpha t/\beta}, $$

where $\bm{\mathrm{c_{1}}}$ and $\bm{\mathrm{c_{2}}}$ are constants determined by the initial conditions. Eq. (42) guarantees a damping solution as long as $\alpha>0$ . We plot the CoM drift and velocity under this gauge boundary condition in Fig. 10. This approach avoids the oscillation of CoM around the coordinate origin, but the damping rate of the CoM drift is smaller than the other example.

The black curves end earlier because the CoM displacement gets so large that the simulation crashes.*

The results obtained so far are specific to equal-mass non-spinning systems. In more general cases with non-equal masses and spin precession, the Newtonian measurement of CoM can exhibit circular motion in addition to the linear drift, as indicated by the blue curve in Fig. 11. However, in the new gauge boundary condition, Eq. (16) or (33), we require the orbit-averaged drift coordinate and drift velocity as $\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}$ and $\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}$ , rather than the quantities associated with the circular motion. So we average the CoM coordinate and velocity over that last available orbit during the simulation, and take the averaged quantities $\langle\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{\text{s}}\rangle$ and $\langle\dot{\bm{\mathrm{r}}}_{\bm{\text{s}}}\rangle$ in the boundary condition. Here $\langle f\rangle=\frac{\int^{t}_{t_{0}}f(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}}{t-t_{0}}$ , where $t_{0}$ is found by maximizing the dot product $\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{12}(t)\cdot\bm{\mathrm{r}}_{12}(t_{0})$ over a time window $[t-3\pi/\Omega,t-\pi/\Omega]$ , with $\Omega$ being the orbital angular velocity.

As an illustration, we take the boundary condition Eq. (16) with Eq. (38). We use a system with mass ratio $q=1$ and dimensionless spin parameters $\chi_{1}=(0.1,0.2,0.3)$ and $\chi_{2}=(0.2,0.4,0.1)$ . The initial separation is $29\,M$ and the merger time is around $65000\,M$ . The resulting trajectory is shown as the green curve in Fig. 11, the vectorial displacement of the CoM under the new BC is shown in Fig. 12, and the overall CoM drifting is shown in Fig. 13. The surge of the CoM velocity near merger is expected and physical: it is the kick due to the asymmetry of the BBH system. Testing shows that this approach is effective for mass ratio $q$ up to $8$ and spin $|\chi_{1,2}|$ up to $0.8$ .

*Figure 14: The waveform differences under modified gauge boundary condition Eq. (32) with $\bm{\mathrm{r_{0}}}$ specified by Eq. (38), where $\lambda=1+(R/100)^{2}$ , and original boundary condition Eq. (13) for two systems. We follow the procedure discussed in Sec. IV of [42] to fix the BMS frame, rotation and time shift between the two waveforms.*

In theory, modification to a gauge boundary condition should not have any impact on waveforms. However, it is crucial to check this. The conclusion should be general to all waveforms, not specific to a single example, since our boundary condition treatments do not depend on the intrinsic parameters of the system like masses and spins.

It is worth noting that the BBH system exhibits asymptotically flat behavior. Bondi, van der Burg, Metzner, and Sachs [39, 40, 13] demonstrated that the spacetime symmetry at the asymptotic boundary can be described by the Bondi-van der Burg-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) group. This BMS group characterizes the asymptotic symmetry of spacetimes that are asymptotically flat at null infinity. Refs. [31, 42] showed the importance of having both waveforms in the same BMS frame for making accurate comparisons. We follow their process to map waveforms obtained using CCE to the same BMS frame using the scri package [15] and the NRPNHybridization code [43].

After fixing the BMS frame and performing the required 3-D rotation and time alignment, we observe that the time-domain mismatch between the waveforms obtained under the Sommerfeld gauge boundary condition and our new gauge boundary condition for the equal-mass and non-spinning system over a $10000\,M$ window is on the order of $10^{-12}$ , and for the precessing system over a $60000\,M$ window is on the order of $10^{-7}$ . The residual is depicted in Fig. 14 for these two cases. This mismatch is much smaller than the numerical error between different resolutions, since the numerical error is dominated by the grid spacing, and we are not changing the grids when modifying the boundary condition. The mismatch is consistent with the tolerance of BMS frame fixing and rotation alignment. So there is no evidence suggesting that the modification of the gauge boundary condition can affect the waveform, once all the gauge ambiguities are fixed. This is as expected since we only modify the gauge part of the boundary conditions.

## VII Alternative Boundary Conditions

#### VII.0.1 Bayliss-Turkel condition

Since Fig. 3 shows that the Sommerfeld boundary condition is only non-reflective for the $\ell=0$ mode, a straightforward idea is to use higher-order boundary conditions that are non-reflective for higher $\ell$ modes. Such boundary conditions are known as Bayliss-Turkel boundary conditions [5]. They are given by

$$ B_{k}\psi\doteq 0, $$

where

$$ B_{k}=\Pi^{k}_{\ell}\left(\partial_{t}+\partial_{r}+\frac{2\ell-1}{r}\right). $$

However, given the presence of the high order derivatives, the well-posedness of these high-order boundary conditions when applied to the first order Generalized-Harmonic evolution [26] is not yet proven.

Here we test the second-order Bayliss-Turkel boundary condition. In terms of incoming characteristic fields in SpEC, it can be written as

$$ P_{ab}^{\mathrm{G}cd}\left[\partial_{t}u_{cd}^{1-}-\partial_{t}\partial_{r}g_{cd}-\partial_{r}^{2}(g_{cd}-g^{\text{background}}_{cd})\right.\\
+\left(\gamma_{2}-\frac{4}{r}\right)\partial_{t}g_{cd}-\frac{4}{r}\partial_{r}(g_{cd}-g^{\text{background}}_{cd})\\
\left.-\frac{2}{r^{2}}(g_{cd}-g^{\text{background}}_{cd})\right]\doteq 0. $$

Here the first derivatives of the metric are computed using the fundamental variables $\Phi$ and $\Pi$ in the first-order GH system [26], and the second derivatives of the metric are computed from derivatives of $\Phi$ and $\Pi$ . To approximate $g^{\text{background}}$ , we tried using the Minkowski metric, the Schwarzschild metric, and the metric used in the initial condition. However, in all cases, there were large junk reflections that caused discontinuities in both CoM velocity and CoM drift, and even led to simulation crashes. This raises concerns about the suitability of the second-order Bayliss-Turkel boundary conditions for BBH simulations in SpEC.

An alternative approach to implement the Bayliss-Turkel type boundary condition without using the background metric is to introduce auxiliary variables defined on the outer boundary that evolve via a simple ODE system [18]. These variables represent the residuals of the Bayliss–Turkel type absorbing operator Eq. (44) for each $l,m$ mode at each order $k$ . Driving them consistently to zero enforces the higher-order absorbing condition. In [18], the higher-order absorbing condition is only imposed on the physical degrees of freedom, and it is shown that the coordinate drift of CoM is not reduced. We leave further investigation of imposing higher-order boundary conditions on the gauge degrees of freedom for future studies.

#### VII.0.2 Gauge constraint damping condition

The gauge constraint damping boundary condition[27] explicitly drives the incoming characteristic fields on the outer boundary to satisfy the gauge condition $\mathcal{C}_{a}=H_{a}-\nabla^{c}\nabla_{c}x_{a}\rightarrow 0$ .

The gauge constraint damping boundary condition can be written as

$$ d_{t}u^{1-}\doteq-\mu_{B}\left(u^{1-}-u^{1-}|_{\text{BC}}\right), $$

where $\mu_{B}$ is a freely chosen damping parameter that exponentially suppresses any constraint violation crossing the boundary, and $u_{ab}^{1-}l^{b}|_{\text{BC}}$ is chosen so that the incoming characteristic projection of the constraint fields $\mathcal{C}_{a}$ vanishes. In terms of the characteristic variables in SpEC, the gauge constraint damping boundary condition reads

$$ \displaystyle P^{\text{G}cd}_{ab}d_{t}u_{cd}^{1-} \displaystyle\doteq-\mu_{B}P^{\text{G}cd}_{ab}\left(u^{1-}_{cd}-u^{1-}_{cd}|_{\text{BC}}\right) \displaystyle\doteq\frac{\mu_{B}}{\sqrt{2}}\left(k_{a}k_{b}l^{c}+k_{a}\delta_{b}^{c}+k_{b}\delta_{a}^{c}\right)\left(\delta_{c}^{d}-t_{c}t^{d}\right)\mathcal{C}_{d}. $$

Please refer to Appendix E of Ref. [27] for details.

The gauge constraint damping boundary condition should be effective at suppressing violations of the GH gauge constraints at the outer boundary [27]. Nevertheless, this condition does not enforce a purely outgoing wave: the gauge condition Eq. (11) still admits both ingoing and outgoing gauge modes, so reflections can still occur in practice. Fig. 15 compares the CoM drift and its velocity for an equal-mass, non-spinning system with an initial separation of $29\,M$ , and the merger time is around $50000\,M$ . Evolution that uses the gauge constraint damping boundary condition (blue curves) exhibits an even larger drift than the result obtained using the original Sommerfeld condition (black curves), indicating that the gauge constraint damping boundary condition does not reduce the reflection from the outer boundary and therefore fails to reduce the CoM drift.

#### VII.0.3 Multipolar post-Minkowskian (MPM)

Another potential approach to reduce the CoM drift is to impose the boundary condition with analytic data supplied by the multipolar post-Minkowskian (MPM) expansion [46, 7, 12, 9]. Ref. [8] gives the multipolar post-Minkowskian metric in Bondi coordinates, expressed entirely in terms of the source’s mass and current multipole moments. By mapping the NR Cauchy coordinates to the Bondi frame using the CCE procedure developed in [34], one can evaluate the MPM solution on the outer boundary and supply it as time-dependent boundary data for the Cauchy evolution. Because this analytically matched metric already satisfies the correct outgoing-radiation behavior, it should suppress gauge reflections at the boundary and is therefore expected to reduce the CoM drift. This procedure is significantly more complicated than other methods discussed here, so we leave it for future studies.

#### VII.0.4 Cauchy-Characteristic matching (CCM)

Alternatively, Cauchy-Characteristic matching (CCM) [23, 6, 29, 28] can also provide accurate physical boundary conditions for the Cauchy domain by performing a matching of the internal Cauchy system and the exterior characteristic system. But currently only the physical part of the fields is matched for BBH systems [29, 28]. Using CCM for the gauge part of the fields is a promising approach to reduce the CoM drift, and we leave this also for future studies.

## VIII Conclusions

In this paper, we analyze the exponential drift of the CoM during long NR simulations of BBH systems. We have demonstrated that this drift is primarily caused by the reflection due to the gauge outer boundary conditions. To understand this issue, in the post-Newtonian approximation we have derived the equation of motion for the CoM under various versions of the gauge boundary conditions.

To mitigate the drift, we propose a modification of the boundary conditions by introducing CoM source terms. The specific form of the source term is not unique, and we present two specific examples showing that the CoM drift can be reduced by several orders of magnitude by incorporating these source terms into the gauge boundary condition.
